comments.text:
Reference gate — 2026-08-04

Contracts and consumer: this slice changes the owner/proof surface of ORB-C4, ORB-C6, and ORB-C7 while preserving their accepted ORBF v1 bytes; it enables Venus VEN-C1 through VEN-C4 without changing a Venus contract. The accepted product proof is e4fde443e625180d7332eff4dff366f64bee30a8 and the pre-edit repository revision is 10a24532c00a8ea11f90055f6ce20858146e42d0.

Required before code:
- Orbit itself at accepted proof e4fde443e625180d7332eff4dff366f64bee30a8 and current 10a24532c00a8ea11f90055f6ce20858146e42d0. Inspected the complete manifest and presentation owner, including the live Extractor/Encoder/OutputQueue path and the test-only Decoder/Frame/read_frame/reattach proof. Independently useful fact: ORBF v1 already has one deterministic complete-frame byte layout and bounded producer limits, but the encoder is private and the only decoder is test-only. Consequence: move the format constants, owned frame value types, bounded encode/decode validation, and revision reduction into one package; leave libghostty extraction, PTY/session authority, Unix transport, and output scheduling in the Orbit binary.
- libghostty-vt 0.2.1, crates.io checksum 6219ed1c364b3ef5815fb0fd2acc0662f792adc706dabf59b7ca89280ee6d066, MIT OR Apache-2.0. Inspected its public Terminal/RenderState surfaces and its global/per-row dirty model. Independently useful fact: libghostty remains the single terminal-semantics owner and can supply complete structured state now plus dirty-row evidence later. Consequence: orbit-protocol must contain no libghostty type or dependency; Orbit alone maps libghostty state into protocol-owned values. Dirty/patch semantics are not introduced by this extraction.
- FrankenTUI at 479436597890a14e82676d0067e3917b2a9de8f5 is routed as required by docs/REFERENCES.md for presentation-proof changes. Its LICENSE is a custom “MIT License (with OpenAI/Anthropic Rider)” that expressly withholds analysis/use rights from OpenAI and agents acting for it. It is therefore license-incompatible for this Codex run: no source, dependency, schema, or implementation-derived mechanism will enter Orbit. Inspection stopped as implementation evidence at the incompatibility. The deterministic transition, headless, golden/property, and one-writer requirements already present in Orbit’s own contracts remain requirements and are independently corroborated below.

Comparison only:
- WezTerm at 577474d89ee61aef4a48145cdec82a638d874751, MIT. Inspected codec render-change types, server change calculation, and client render cache. Stable row indices, seqno-based invalidation, viewport-adjacent bonus rows, and separately hydrated image data are useful evidence that future partial frames need explicit baseline/cache semantics. Rejected for ORBF v1: no multiplexer surface, lazy history fetch, client terminal cache, image side channel, or patch format enters this complete-frame extraction.
- justerm at 0e468a7fde4e75d307983258d09dd8dfbe26f81a, MIT OR Apache-2.0. Inspected its frame/wire map, damage ADR, decoder ownership, and FrameSource seam. Independently useful mechanism: bind consumers to a decoded format-owned frame and reuse the canonical decoder across targets instead of maintaining a second schema. Rejected surrounding scope: no justerm schema, terminal engine, span/damage model, web mirror, WASM package, ack protocol, scroll op, overlay model, or renderer code.
- Mosh state synchronization is comparison evidence for latest-revision convergence and obsolete-intermediate-state reduction. It does not authorize remote transport, prediction, acknowledgement flow control, visible-screen replication, or a new state-sync protocol.

Conditional references:
- cargo-fuzz is conditional only if deterministic malformed/truncated/allocation-hostile checks expose a decoder risk that cannot be bounded economically in normal tests.
- RDP frame acknowledgement is conditional only on measured slow-client pressure that requires receiver feedback. Neither condition is present in this slice.

Rejected as unrelated scope: vt100 and termwiz terminal engines, zmx bootstrap/tail attachment, any client-side VT parser, schema generator, generic protocol framework, compatibility adapter, trace format, remote transport, or renderer.

License result: Orbit and libghostty are project/existing dependency evidence; WezTerm is MIT; justerm is MIT OR Apache-2.0; FrankenTUI is incompatible for this run and contributes nothing to the implementation. No source will be copied from any reference.

Ownership and code shape: a platform-neutral, std-only orbit-protocol library owns ORBF v1 constants, bounded owned value types, strict encode/decode, errors, and complete-frame revision validation/reduction. The root yazelix-orbit package remains the only owner of libghostty, PTYs, sockets, connection order, and extraction. Venus will consume this package at one exact accepted Orbit Git revision and will not mirror the wire schema.

First meaningful contract check: decode the accepted rich ORBF v1 corpus, re-encode it byte-for-byte, reject malformed/truncated/trailing/allocation-hostile payloads before unbounded allocation, and reject a stale or duplicate complete-frame revision while accepting a strictly newer revision. Platform classification: neutral.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Crate gate — accepted dependency and package decision — 2026-08-04

Decision already authorized by the user after the protocol-boundary stop: add one internal, dependency-free, platform-neutral orbit-protocol workspace library and make yazelix-orbit depend on it by path. Do not add an external crate, publish target, schema generator, compatibility window, fourth repository, or second decoder. This gate records the comparison behind that accepted choice; it does not expand the approval.

Affected contracts: ORB-C4, ORB-C6, and ORB-C7; Venus will consume the exact accepted Orbit Git revision for VEN-C1 through VEN-C4. Existing product dependencies remain libc 0.2.189 and libghostty-vt 0.2.1 in the root binary only.

Candidate matrix:

1. Selected — internal std-only orbit-protocol package with the existing explicit little-endian ORBF v1 codec.
Fit/ownership: exact fit; one format owner, reusable by Orbit and Venus, no PTY/terminal dependency leakage, no wire revision. Estimated code movement is the existing roughly 60-line encoder plus roughly 100-line test decoder, with owned public values, errors, reducer, and focused tests added in the same package; no duplicated schema. Cost: one direct workspace path edge, zero external direct/transitive/native/build/Nix dependencies, no proc macros, no generated files. API/versioning: private Git-pinned package, publish=false, explicit VERSION=1 and strict errors; Orbit controls upgrades with its proof commit. License/security: project-owned; checked arithmetic and pre-allocation bounds can match the exact hostile-input contract. Platform: std-only byte/value logic is neutral across Linux, macOS, and a future wasm32 consumer. Accessibility/input/browser: no policy or OS API is embedded, so those remain consumer concerns.

2. Root library target with terminal features, no new package.
Fit/ownership: can expose a decoder but couples consumer resolution to the yazelix-orbit package and its libc/libghostty build graph unless terminal dependencies become optional features. That feature split adds manifest states and makes it easier for protocol and terminal ownership to drift within one crate. Project LOC is superficially smaller but consumer/build isolation is worse. Rejected because the acceptance criterion requires a consumer build that cannot compile PTY, libc, libghostty, or governance code.

3. Keep the encoder private and hand Venus a separate decoder.
Fit/ownership: zero dependency cost but creates the forbidden second schema and makes byte drift invisible until cross-repository integration. Rejected by the Orbit/Venus ownership contract.

4. bincode 2.0.1, MIT (the crates.io latest, 3.0.0, is a deliberately nonfunctional compile_error placeholder and is not a credible candidate).
Fit: mature general Rust binary codec, but its derived representation is not accepted ORBF v1; preserving v1 would still need the owned parser/encoder. Default 2.0.1 adds bincode_derive and unty, with proc-macro/build graph; serde is another optional edge. Owned LOC is not removed for the existing format. Pure Rust and broadly portable, but upgrades/configuration become wire decisions. Rejected: dependency cost and format instability for zero contract gain.

5. postcard 1.1.3, MIT OR Apache-2.0.
Fit: compact/no_std serde format, but it changes bytes and needs serde plus cobs and default heapless support; preserving ORBF again leaves a custom adapter. Pure Rust, macOS/wasm credible, no native dependency, but its embedded-oriented framing and serde data model do not prove the terminal-specific bounds or exact accepted revision. Rejected: more transitive and upgrade surface without removing the canonical codec.

6. prost 0.14.4 / Protocol Buffers, Apache-2.0.
Fit: mature schema evolution and multi-language ecosystem, but ORBF v1 is not protobuf. It adds bytes and prost-derive at runtime and normally prost-build plus a .proto/generated source workflow at build time; that increases build, cache, Nix, and upgrade surfaces and creates generated artifacts. Browser interoperability is strong in a different protocol, but no remote or general multi-language protocol is authorized. Rejected: wire change, generator, schema compatibility surface, and materially greater cost.

7. rkyv 0.8.17, MIT.
Fit: high-performance archive/zero-copy model, but archived Rust layout, alignment/pointer-width choices, validation, and its broad dependency set are unnecessary for a small bounded network frame and make cross-target stability a larger concern. Defaults include bytecheck plus derive and supporting crates such as hashbrown, munge, ptr_meta, rancor, and rend. No native build is required, but compile/upgrade/security review cost is highest of the pure-Rust candidates. Rejected: no measured zero-copy pressure, wrong stability shape, changes bytes.

8. capnp 0.27.0 / Cap’n Proto, MIT.
Fit: explicit schema and cross-language evolution, but requires a new wire and generated bindings; normal development adds capnpc/schema compilation and may require the external capnp tool, creating build and Nix/platform cost. It is credible for a future separately approved multi-language/remote protocol, not for exact v1 extraction. Rejected.

9. Separate protocol repository/package publication.
Fit: strongest physical isolation but adds a fourth version/release/coordination surface and conflicts with the accepted exact-Git-revision consumption model. Rejected by the user-approved scope.

Focused proof and disputed claims: cargo info and normalized crates.io manifests were inspected for bincode 2.0.1/3.0.0, postcard 1.1.3, prost 0.14.4, rkyv 0.8.17, and capnp 0.27.0. bincode 3.0.0 contains compile_error!("https://xkcd.com/2347/"). The accepted e4fde443 Orbit source proves the existing format already has a compact encoder and test decoder, so an external serializer removes no required v1 logic.

Consequences of the accepted choice: Cargo.toml adds crates/protocol as a workspace member and orbit-protocol as a root path dependency; crates/protocol/Cargo.toml declares edition 2024 and publish=false with no dependencies. Cargo.lock should only gain the local package edge. docs/CRATES.md will record this durable decision. Root production maps libghostty state into protocol-owned values; the protocol crate never imports libghostty, libc, sockets, renderer APIs, platform APIs, or governance. The first check is an exact accepted rich-frame decode/re-encode plus bounded hostile-input and strict revision tests, followed by cargo tree/metadata evidence that orbit-protocol has no external dependency graph.

title: Decide whether Orbit should retain its diagnostic client
description:
## Contract routing

This is a planning-only developer-surface decision. It changes no ORB product contract, executable behavior, CLI, documentation, or tests. Any chosen removal or relocation requires a separately authorized implementation Bead and explicit treatment of the existing public command spelling.

Consumer: Orbit maintainers debugging the canonical local session protocol; no current Eon or Venus runtime consumer is known.

Trigger: determine whether `yazelix-orbit client [SOCKET]` still provides unique diagnostic value after Venus and the real lifecycle/protocol integration suites became canonical consumers.

Result: record one evidence-backed decision to retain, shrink, relocate to test/example tooling, or remove the client, including the smallest surviving diagnostic path and all user-visible/doc consequences.

Important failures: do not infer zero external use only from local callers; do not remove the shared canonical codec; do not keep production CLI solely because it was useful before Venus existed.

## Why

The installed Orbit binary still exposes an interactive line-oriented diagnostic client. `run_client` connects and negotiates ORBS, converts each stdin line into Paste plus Enter, and prints server messages. The path is roughly 85 production LOC and appears unused by Eon, Venus, or the automated lifecycle suite, but it may remain the cheapest manual protocol probe.

Impact: LOW. Investigation effort: S. Decision risk: LOW. Confidence in removal opportunity: MED-HIGH.

## Evidence

- `src/main.rs:274-301`: public CLI dispatch exposes `client [SOCKET]` beside the production `serve` mode.
- `src/main.rs:546-628`: `run_client`, client-message writing, server-message reading, and diagnostic printing implement the interactive path.
- `README.md:13-25`: current product description still names the diagnostic client and canonical protocol use.
- `docs/RATIONALE.md:332-347`: historical sequencing retains a headless runtime and diagnostic client used by the initial proof.
- Repository search finds no Eon, Eonova, Venus, or Orbit test invocation of the installed `client` command; automated tests use their own typed fixtures/clients.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- Record exact Orbit, Eon, Eon Desktop, and Eonova revisions inspected.
- Trace every local caller and documentation reference to the `client` command and its helper functions.
- Search known consumer repositories and package wrappers for invocation of `yazelix-orbit client`; distinguish absence in known sources from a compatibility promise to unknown users.
- Compare its unique debugging capability with `tests/lifecycle.rs`, protocol unit tests, Venus transport/integration tests, and ordinary socket/protocol fixtures.
- Check release/documentation history to determine whether the command is an accepted public surface, a developer-only experiment, or merely installed incidentally.

## Scope

In scope:
- `src/main.rs` CLI branch, `run_client`, and helpers used only by that branch.
- README/rationale/contracts/package references to the diagnostic client.
- Known Eon, Venus, Eonova, CI, and test consumers.
- Retain, shrink, test/example relocation, and removal shapes.

Out of scope:
- Editing runtime code, docs, tests, packages, or contracts.
- Removing or weakening the ORBS codec, server behavior, Venus attachment, or real lifecycle tests.
- Designing a new debugging UI, protocol inspector, TUI, logging system, or compatibility layer.
- Adding dependencies or a new published binary.
- Assuming support for unknown external consumers without evidence.

## Decision method

1. Inventory the exact production LOC/imports/branches owned only by the diagnostic client and any code shared with the server.
2. Inventory actual consumers and the unique troubleshooting questions the command can answer.
3. Compare four shapes: retain unchanged; shrink the existing command; move equivalent probing into test/example tooling; remove it and rely on canonical consumers/tests.
4. For each shape, assess installed surface area, maintenance with future ORBS changes, manual diagnostic utility, automated coverage, documentation cost, and compatibility risk.
5. Select the first sufficient shape; name exact retained capability, rejected alternatives, and the event that would reverse the decision.
6. If change is selected, specify the smallest later implementation slice and changelog/documentation obligations, but create no implementation Bead without separate user authorization.

## Acceptance

- Every local and known cross-repository consumer is accounted for.
- The record states whether `client` is a supported user-facing command, developer tool, or obsolete experiment and cites the evidence.
- Unique manual diagnostic value is demonstrated with a concrete workflow or rejected as already covered.
- The decision explicitly chooses retain, shrink, relocate, or remove and quantifies owned LOC/surface consequences.
- Any removal decision names the exact helpers/imports/docs affected and how maintainers perform the remaining necessary diagnosis.
- Any retain decision states why production CLI ownership is cheaper than existing test/example mechanisms.
- The Bead records rejected alternatives, compatibility limits, reversal conditions, and whether later implementation is warranted.

## Verification

- `rg -n 'run_client|Some\("client"\)|yazelix-orbit client|diagnostic client' README.md docs src tests .github Cargo.toml` should enumerate all local references.
- Equivalent searches in the checked-out Eon, Eon Desktop, and Eonova repositories should enumerate known consumers.
- `cargo test --locked --workspace` should establish the current canonical protocol/lifecycle baseline; it does not by itself prove the interactive command unused.
- If retained value is claimed, record one exact manual workflow and its observed unique signal without modifying repository state.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0; implementation and documentation files must remain unchanged.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue for this Bead.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only authorized planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if a known runtime, CI job, or supported external workflow consumes the command and removal policy needs a user compatibility decision.
- Stop if the command or ORBS revision changes during investigation; record the new snapshot and restart the analysis.
- Stop if evaluating an alternative requires source edits or a new diagnostic feature.
- Stop if removal would weaken canonical server, protocol, or lifecycle verification.

## Maintenance notes

Do not replace 85 production LOC with a similarly sized custom example. If automated tests already answer the necessary questions, deletion is the smallest shape; if live manual probing is genuinely unique, retain the production command deliberately.
notes:
Decision — 2026-08-14: remove the installed diagnostic client in a separately authorized implementation Bead. This decision changes no product contract and makes no runtime, documentation, test, or manifest edit.

Classification: the client is a documented proof-era developer probe, not a supported product command. It was introduced with the first PTY-lifetime proof; Eon packages the binary but invokes only serve, Venus consumes canonical ORBS directly, Eonova consumes the packaged composition, and no known runtime, package, test, or CI path invokes client. The private repository has no tags, releases, or forks.

Selected shape: delete the client CLI arm, client-only BufRead and BufReader imports, run_client, and print_server_message; reduce the usage text to serve. The current branch and client/helper/printing region is about 82 source lines: about 62 client-only lines can disappear, while write_client_message and read_server_message remain useful to strong tests and should become test-only rather than be duplicated. Update current README and rationale wording, preserve or clarify only necessary historical contract wording, and record the user-visible command removal in CHANGELOG when accepted. The implementation changes no ORB contract but touches the shared owner surface, so it must classify and reprove ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 as preserved.

Why: the exact live probe accepts a socket, maps every stdin line to Paste plus Enter, and prints attachment, acknowledgements, failures, exit, and frame revision/size/title. It does not print terminal cells or the submitted shell output, cannot express most accepted semantic messages, mutates the session, and occupies the sole client slot. Venus is the complete live manual consumer. The canonical lifecycle and presentation tests provide stronger deterministic negotiation, input, detach/reattach, state, failure, and rich-frame signals.

Rejected: retain unchanged keeps obsolete installed and protocol-coupled surface; shrink keeps the same command/compatibility burden for less signal; relocation replaces the deleted code with a similarly sized example and duplicates existing typed test clients.

Reconsider a dedicated tool only after a concrete live-server question cannot be answered by Venus, tests, or normal process/socket diagnostics.

title: Decide Orbit same-boot session hosting and adoption
description:
## Problem

Orbit e60554623d2ad1e238fac84d0f8f49be0e81e522 already survives loss of its graphical client, but it is launched and observed as a std::process::Child of the Eon supervisor. Orbit owns the real PTY and authoritative libghostty state; Eon owns the product Session mapping and lifecycle policy.

This leaves a precise same-boot gap. If Eon exits normally, current stop paths terminate Orbit. If Eon crashes without running cleanup, Orbit may remain as an orphan with a live Unix socket, but a replacement Eon cannot safely prove that the endpoint belongs to the expected Session and generation, observe its authoritative exit, obtain its exit status, stop it through an accepted owner, or distinguish it from stale or replaced state. A PID, pathname, or filesystem record is not process identity.

Decide the minimum process-hosting and local management shape required for a replacement Eon to reconnect to the exact still-running Orbit Session after Eon supervisor loss. This is not machine-restart persistence, topology reconstruction, remote attachment, or multiplayer.

## Contract routing

- This is a deferred decision/research Bead. It changes no ORB-C, EON-C, or VEN-C contract, reserves no contract ID, and authorizes no code, binary, daemon, service unit, dependency, protocol, or packaging change.
- The Eon product decision eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf must first select exact same-boot supervisor-loss continuity.
- If selected, approve and index the smallest user-visible Orbit lifecycle/management contract before implementation. Preserve ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 and the one active presentation client.
- Orbit remains the only PTY process, terminal-state, retained-history, terminal-query, and Session-lifetime authority. Eon remains product identity, topology, selection, and recovery-policy owner. Venus remains transient.
- Keep management identity/status/stop distinct from ORBS presentation attachment. Do not weaken the one-client rule merely to let Eon inspect a live Session.

## Evidence

Current owner flow:

- src/main.rs::run_server creates the local listener, owns Pty and libghostty Terminal, exits on shutdown signal or PTY completion, and removes its exact socket on drop.
- src/platform.rs::Pty creates a new session and controlling PTY for the child; dropping Orbit sends HUP/KILL to the child process groups and reaps the direct child.
- Eon f036f798855668b53fa7e099fcb938ba6f0ffe2f stores every Orbit process as Child, observes it with try_wait, and owns normal stop and workspace pruning. Workspace and Session IDs are in-memory.
- ORBS proves presentation attachment, Busy, exact socket identity during startup, coherent frames, and detach/reconnect. It does not prove management identity, adoption by a new Eon parent, Orbit restart, or machine restart.

Relevant comparisons:

- zmx 4f3739ef98f44d0b639afa57fd76bffcad5d0ef4 and abduco 8c32909a159aaa9484c82b71f05b7a73321eb491 use one daemon/server per session. Per-session failure isolation is useful; their raw-terminal bootstrap, multi-client behavior, command surfaces, labels, and session semantics are rejected.
- shpool 901e18c3ced010073178b78c0ca2a8cdd43e8581 uses one daemon retaining child ownership and ships systemd socket/service units plus macOS launch-service guidance. Its shared daemon is comparison evidence, not an adopted dependency or architecture.
- tmux 851c5a933d4838c32ad06c248b2ba975d106149c uses one background server and stable in-server IDs; official docs state sessions are gone if the server is killed. This demonstrates both clean parenting and the shared failure domain.
- systemd 40315add9176d2a7c28d8d90490f74e9e982e87b can own transient or persistent user services and track their cgroups. loginctl linger can keep the user manager running after logout. This is credible Linux ownership but creates a platform and product-policy seam.
- CRIU is irrelevant to the first decision: the process is already alive. No checkpoint or terminal-state serialization should enter this scope.

## Proposed scope

Compare the mechanism options, recommend one or no change, and define the first contract check. Every option must cover authoritative identity, start convergence, useful-work survival, exit observation, explicit stop, socket recreation or replacement, stale metadata, permissions, version mismatch, partial startup, crash cleanup, logout behavior, and Linux/macOS removal cost.

Out of scope: persistence after Orbit or machine restart; topology or launch-intent storage; remote transport; SSH; cloud sync; history export; graphics; multiple clients; a public protocol; process checkpointing; automatic adoption based only on PID/path/process name; and implementation.
design:
## Options to compare

### Option A — no new behavior

Keep the Eon supervisor as the only launcher/parent and promise durability only while it remains alive. This is the smallest system. Improve diagnostics and wording in the Eon decision, but add no Orbit surface.

### Option B — systemd user service per Orbit Session

Eon requests a transient or generated user service with a stable opaque Session/run identity; systemd owns process and cgroup lifetime, while Orbit remains PTY authority. Eon validates owner-authored Orbit identity before attach and uses service-manager status/stop through one platform seam.

Advantages: mature Linux supervision, crash-independent parenting, bounded start/stop and logs, no project-owned generic daemon. Costs: systemd user-manager availability, linger and runtime-directory policy, unit cleanup, command or D-Bus integration, Nix packaging, Linux-only behavior, and a credible macOS replacement. Do not make a systemd unit name the product Session identity.

### Option C — one portable Eon session broker

A long-lived local broker becomes the parent and wait owner for all Orbit processes; replacement Eon supervisors query it through a private bounded control boundary.

Advantages: correct child exit/status ownership, portable conceptual model, one management endpoint. Costs: new binary/process/protocol, all-Sessions shared failure domain, broker upgrade and restart semantics, resource bounds, and potential duplication of Eon lifecycle ownership. The broker may host processes but must not own terminal or product topology state.

### Option D — self-daemonizing per-session Orbit

Each Orbit process detaches safely from Eon, retains direct PTY-child ownership, and exposes a narrow private management identity/status/stop plane. Replacement Eon discovers candidates, validates exact owner-authored identity, and reconciles them.

Advantages: per-session failure isolation, no shared broker, closest to current one-process-per-Session shape and zmx/abduco evidence. Costs: daemonization/stdio/signal semantics, stable run identity, management concurrency, endpoint recreation, non-parent exit observation, logs, cleanup, and platform launch differences. Do not stretch ORBS presentation negotiation into a second client or let filesystem metadata become authority.

### Option E — Linux pidfd adoption without a durable owner

A replacement Eon validates a run record, opens a pidfd, polls for exit, and signals it through the Linux platform seam.

Potentially small on Linux, but it cannot by itself recover wait-owned exit status and remains vulnerable to incomplete identity/record authority. macOS needs another mechanism. Treat it as a focused primitive inside another accepted shape, not a default product architecture.

### Option F — PID file, process-name scan, or socket-only adoption

Reject. PID reuse, same-path replacement, version mismatch, and stale sockets make these unsafe lifecycle authorities. Files may locate a candidate only; a live owner-authored handshake must validate it.

## First proof shape if selected

Use one isolated Session running a deterministic long-lived command. Kill the Eon supervisor with SIGKILL without signaling Orbit. Start the exact accepted replacement control path, validate the same run and Orbit identity, reattach through canonical ORBS, observe unchanged child PID and terminal state, then request owner-routed stop and prove bounded PTY-group cleanup plus no stale endpoint. Repeat with wrong identity, stale socket, incompatible generation, concurrent recovery, Orbit exit during recovery, and logout behavior. Machine reboot must fail the exact-continuity claim explicitly.

The decision must name the cheapest platform-neutral contract and the narrow Linux process/platform seam.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The final comparison covers no change, per-Session systemd user services, one portable broker, self-daemonizing per-session Orbit, pidfd as a subordinate Linux primitive, and unsafe PID/path adoption.
2. Each viable option assigns one owner for launch, stable run identity, live validation, child exit and exit status, explicit stop, socket lifecycle, normal shutdown, supervisor crash, Orbit crash, abandoned Session cleanup, and version mismatch.
3. Orbit remains sole PTY and terminal-state authority; Eon remains product Session/topology/recovery-policy authority; Venus receives no persistence responsibility.
4. Management and presentation remain separate logical responsibilities. The one active ORBS presentation client is preserved, and no consumer reconstructs terminal state from raw PTY bytes or files.
5. Candidate discovery is non-authoritative until a live owner-authored handshake validates stable Session identity, unique run identity, exact protocol/component generation, process start identity, endpoint identity, and user ownership. PID, socket path, process name, or stored metadata alone cannot authorize attach or stop.
6. The decision defines bounds for startup, handshake, retries, clients, queues, logs, records, shutdown, partial failure, and cleanup, plus permissions and symlink defenses.
7. Every viable option records portability as neutral, isolated platform dependency, or macOS blocker with exact replacement shape and estimated removal cost. systemd and pidfd remain behind a narrow Linux seam.
8. The first proof kills Eon while useful work continues, reattaches a replacement to the same process and authoritative terminal state, then proves owner-routed stop. Negative checks cover stale/replaced endpoints, wrong identity, concurrent recovery, incompatible generation, Orbit exit, and machine reboot.
9. The recommendation names dependency and binary impact, owned LOC estimate, upgrade/removal cost, and evidence that would reverse it. Prefer no new crate and no new process unless the contract cannot be satisfied otherwise.
10. The user approves no change or one mechanism before any contract-index, code, manifest, package, or service-unit edit.
notes:
Planning-only batch authorized on 2026-08-12. No implementation, baseline, Reference gate comment, or Crate gate is required or implied by this decision record.

Priority P2 and deferred. The initial evidence favors comparing Option D against Option B, with Option A as the baseline: per-session ownership fits Orbit failure isolation, while systemd is the strongest Linux native supervisor. A shared broker is justified only if exact exit/status and lifecycle ownership cannot be expressed cleanly per Session.

Required before any later implementation decision: reread AGENTS.md, eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf, exact current Eon lifecycle source and accepted EON-C8/EON-C10/EON-C11 proofs, ORB-C1 through ORB-C11, docs/REFERENCES.md PTY/session-lifetime routing, exact current FrankenTerm lifecycle evidence, zmx, shpool, abduco, tmux, and systemd source. Classify CRIU and remote-compute material as rejected scope.

Related but not prerequisite: orb-permanent-ssh-terminal-access-hd6 consumes a live host Session through SSH and must not claim recovery after the Orbit host or machine is gone.

title: Choose honest ORBS version-mismatch semantics
description:
## Contract routing

This is a planning-only compatibility decision. It changes no ORB product contract, wire bytes, implementation, dependency, or compatibility promise by itself.

Consumer: an exact local ORBS client and Orbit server that need deterministic behavior when their session revisions differ.

Trigger: compare the current exact-version header with the `Hello` version range and typed `Incompatible` messages before the next authorized ORBS revision.

Result: the user selects one coherent policy and owner: either keep exact-version framing and remove or narrow the unreachable range-negotiation surface in the next authorized breaking revision, or authorize a stable bootstrap envelope with explicitly bounded compatibility semantics. Record the update order for Orbit, Venus, and Eon/Eonova.

Important failures: do not silently add dual-version support, an adapter, a compatibility window, or a feature-probe framework; do not claim typed incompatibility when the peer cannot decode it.

## Why

ORBS v3 rejects a non-v3 header before decoding the `Hello` payload, yet the typed API advertises version-range overlap and `Incompatible`. A real v2 or future peer cannot reach that path or decode the v3 response. The current exact pin limits exposure but leaves dead compatibility flexibility and misleading failure semantics.

Impact: MED. Investigation effort: S. Decision risk: HIGH because the selected shape governs future wire compatibility. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:141-174`: `Hello` and `Incompatible` describe inclusive revision-range negotiation.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:572-597`: `message_len` rejects a header whose version differs from `VERSION` before message-kind or payload decoding.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:731-743`: the Hello range becomes available only after exact-header validation.
- `src/main.rs:653-672`: an actual header mismatch becomes generic `FailureCode::Protocol`.
- `src/main.rs:705-726`: typed `Incompatible` is reachable only for a current-header Hello whose payload range excludes v3.
- `tests/lifecycle.rs:455-470`: the incompatibility test uses the current encoder/header, so it does not exercise a stale or future header.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:110-119`: accepted v1-to-v2 and v2-to-v3 changes deliberately selected no adapter, dual decoder, feature probe, or compatibility window.
- Audit `orb-audit-orbit-protocols-bkk` recorded the issue at Orbit `7d34399b15496513f7f91b94acd32e8d04389e16`.

## Reference classification

Required:

- Current `AGENTS.md`, this complete Bead, `docs/CONTRACTS.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md`, `docs/RATIONALE.md`, `docs/CRATES.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Exact ORBS v1, v2, and v3 protocol sources and the accepted `orb-bi4.10`, `orb-j0m.3`, and `orb-ll1.1` decisions/proofs.
- Exact current Venus and Eon/Eonova pins plus their user-visible handling of protocol mismatch.
- Any then-active or selected next-revision protocol Bead, including `orb-orbit-typed-wheel-outcomes-5nq` and deferred `orb-j2i`, only to establish serialization and avoid conflicting revision ownership.

Comparison only:

- One or two mature local protocols with a stable bootstrap/version-negotiation envelope, if needed to falsify or specify that option. Record exact identities and adopt no surrounding transport, RPC, schema, or compatibility framework.

Rejected scope:

- Remote transport, capability negotiation, multiple simultaneous protocol decoders, indefinite backwards compatibility, a generic RPC handshake, or a new dependency.

## Scope

In scope:

- The current ORBS header, `Hello`, `Attached`, `Incompatible`, and protocol-failure flow.
- Known Orbit, Venus, and Eon/Eonova consumers and exact update ordering.
- A comparison of the minimum coherent policy shapes and their wire/LOC/test consequences.
- The first runnable check and a separately authorizable implementation slice if a change is selected.

Out of scope:

- Editing code, tests, manifests, docs, contracts, or protocol bytes.
- Choosing the next product feature or activating any open/deferred protocol feature.
- Implementing compatibility, adding a dependency, or creating implementation children before the user decision.
- Reworking non-version session messages.

## Decision method

1. Reproduce the exact mismatch: encode `Hello`, mutate only header bytes 4..6 to `VERSION - 1` while its payload range includes `VERSION`, and record that header validation prevents negotiation.
2. Trace what the exact current Venus client can decode or display for both older-server and newer-server cases.
3. Compare complete shapes:
   - retain exact-version framing and simplify the next authorized revision to exact `Hello`/attachment with header mismatch as a transport-level incompatibility;
   - retain the current range types as reserved but explicitly stop claiming cross-header negotiation;
   - define a stable minimal bootstrap envelope for future revisions, with exact support bounds and update order;
   - any smaller source-evidenced alternative.
4. For each shape, record public/wire semantics, decoder count, owned LOC, allocation bounds, failure UX, test surface, rollout order, removal cost, and interaction with already planned protocol revisions.
5. Recommend the first sufficient shape. Ponytail bias: exact pins plus the simplest honest failure surface unless a demonstrated supported workflow needs negotiable compatibility.
6. Stop for the user's explicit compatibility decision. If change is selected, specify one bounded Orbit-owner implementation Bead followed by separately owned consumer adoption; create neither in this run.

Portability disposition: neutral.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The current mismatch is reproduced with exact bytes and both peer directions are traced through the known consumers.
2. The record explains why today's typed `Incompatible` is or is not decodable by a different-header peer.
3. At least exact-framing simplification and stable-bootstrap shapes are compared without assuming a compatibility requirement.
4. The selected recommendation names one header/version owner, exact failure semantics, known consumers, update order, old-revision disposition, and whether it changes an indexed contract.
5. No adapter, window, second decoder, feature probe, dependency, or implementation is implied unless the user explicitly selects it.
6. The decision records rejected alternatives, reversal conditions, first falsifying check, effort/risk, and interaction with other planned ORBS revisions.
7. Repository files remain unchanged; only this Bead's planning record is updated.

## Verification

- `cargo test --locked -p orbit-protocol` should establish the current codec baseline.
- Run the focused byte-mutation reproduction in a disposable test/proof surface and record its exact result without editing production files.
- `rg -n 'Hello|Incompatible|UnsupportedVersion|client_message_len|server_message_len' crates/protocol/src/session.rs src tests docs` should enumerate local owners and claims.
- Exact searches in Venus and Eon/Eonova should enumerate consumers and mismatch UX.
- `cargo test --locked --workspace` should exit 0 on the unchanged decision subject.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0 with no implementation or documentation change.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if another active issue owns the same ORBS header/version decision.
- Stop if current source or consumer pins change; record a new subject and repeat the trace.
- Stop before any contract, protocol, code, test, manifest, or consumer edit.
- Stop if a compatibility promise, cross-repository update, or new dependency would be required without explicit user approval.

## Maintenance notes

This decision should be resolved before intentionally minting another ORBS revision, but it is not a blocker for read-only audits. Do not preserve range fields merely because they already exist; preserve only a demonstrated compatibility contract.
notes:
Decision accepted 2026-08-13: exact-version framing.

The canonical ORBS header VERSION is the sole version owner. title: Decide whole PTY-session shutdown ownership
description:
## Contract Routing

This is a planning-only Orbit lifecycle-policy decision. It changes no ORB product contract, implementation, dependency, protocol, or compatibility promise by itself.

Consumer: a local user explicitly terminating an Orbit Session directly or through Eon/EonTerm.

Trigger: Orbit receives an accepted shutdown signal while its PTY session contains a HUP-ignoring job-control process group distinct from both the initial child group and the current foreground group.

Result: the user chooses whether explicit Session shutdown owns and reaps every process group in the PTY session or intentionally permits distinct groups to survive, with exact observable semantics and owner-routed proof.

Important failures: no accidental survivor under a successful full-stop claim, PID-reuse-prone broad scan, unrelated process termination, unbounded cleanup, duplicate Eon ownership, or silent expansion into machine-restart persistence.

Impact: MED. Decision effort: M. Implementation risk: HIGH. Confidence: HIGH.

## Why

Orbit currently signals only the initial child process group and one foreground-group snapshot. POSIX job control permits other process groups in the same session. A HUP-ignoring background group therefore survives a clean Orbit shutdown. The present ORB-C1 wording does not explicitly say whether full-session shutdown owns that group, so this is a contract choice before it is an implementation bug.

## Evidence

- `src/platform.rs:112-127`: shutdown sends HUP/KILL only to the initial child group and one `tcgetpgrp` result.
- Negative `kill` targets one process group, not an entire session.
- Closed audit `orb-audit-orbit-platform-t4s`, finding F3, at source `750490f40f348b66aa8809c66c40587ca8db741f`: a real shell enabled job control, ignored HUP, and started `sleep` in a distinct background group. After SIGTERM and clean Orbit exit, PID 337993 survived reparented to PID 1 until the audit killed it.
- Closed integration audit `orb-audit-orbit-integration-ur9` distinguishes this from Eon's SIGKILL bypass: this finding remains even after Orbit cleanup is allowed to run.
- Deferred `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu` asks who hosts/adopts Orbit after Eon loss; it is related but does not decide explicit shutdown of all job-control groups.

## Reference Classification

Required:

- Current `AGENTS.md`, this complete Bead, ORB-C1 and adjacent lifecycle contracts, `docs/REFERENCES.md` process-lifecycle route, `docs/RATIONALE.md`, `docs/CRATES.md`, exact cleanup code/tests, and both audit records.
- Exact Linux/POSIX session, process-group, controlling-terminal, signal, and reaping semantics recorded by the platform audit.
- Exact Process Triage reference for observe-plan-apply, protected boundaries, staged action, and verification—without importing its general process-classification scope.
- Exact zmx, shpool, and abduco cleanup behavior only for the same explicit-session-shutdown question.

Comparison only:

- Current process-group cleanup.
- Kernel/session supervision mechanisms that can identify and verify only the owned Session processes.
- `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu` and Eon `eon-choose-orbit-owned-shutdown-zmn` solely to keep lifecycle decisions coherent.

Rejected scope:

- `/proc` or process-name scans as authority, killing an entire user subtree, system-wide cleanup, remote/machine-restart persistence, a shared broker, new daemon, new dependency, or Eon-owned PTY cleanup.

## Decision Method

1. Re-run the exact distinct-background-group reproduction and record initial, foreground, background, session, and parent identities before and after shutdown.
2. Compare:
   - Explicit shutdown owns all process groups in the Orbit-created PTY session, with a verifiable platform mechanism and bounded escalation.
   - Explicit shutdown owns only direct/foreground groups and reports/document the permitted survivor semantics honestly.
   - A supervisor/cgroup-hosted shape only if safe whole-session cleanup cannot be expressed within Orbit's current process authority.
3. For each shape, name the user-visible Stop result, owner of discovery/identity/signal/reap/timeout, ORB-C1 effect or new-contract need, Eon/EonTerm consequence, Linux/macOS replacement shape, failure modes, owned LOC, and first check.
4. Prefer no new process/dependency. Reject broad scans and duplicate Eon cleanup.
5. Stop for the user's explicit lifecycle-policy choice.
6. If full-session cleanup is selected, create one bounded Orbit implementation Bead and make any Eon acceptance work consume its proof.

Portability disposition: isolated platform dependency; the policy should be platform-neutral, while Linux and macOS need independently proved process/session mechanisms.

## Scope

In scope:

- Explicit shutdown semantics for PTY-session job-control groups.
- Contract/owner/update-order decision and first real process proof.
- Relationship to same-boot adoption and Eon cooperative shutdown.

Out of scope:

- Code/docs/contracts edits, implementation children, supervisor-crash adoption, remote/machine restart, persistence, socket races, transient EIO, or stopping existing user Sessions.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The exact survivor is reproduced and all relevant process/session/group identities are recorded.
2. The decision states whether accepted explicit shutdown permits or forbids distinct background-group survivors.
3. One owner is named for identity, enumeration, signaling, escalation, reaping/verification, timeout, and result reporting.
4. Full-session, permitted-survivor, and supervisor-hosted fallback shapes are compared without assuming a new daemon or dependency.
5. The decision names ORB-C1/new-contract implications, Eon/EonTerm effects, exact consumer update order, portability disposition, first check, effort/risk, and reversal condition.
6. Broad PID/process-name scans, Eon-owned cleanup, unrelated-process killing, and unbounded waits are rejected.
7. No implementation or contract change occurs before explicit user approval.
8. Only this planning record changes; related decisions are linked without false blocking dependencies.

## Verification

- Re-run the isolated HUP-ignoring background-group reproduction without repository edits and clean every spawned process.
- `rg -n 'stop_and_reap|tcgetpgrp|kill\(|install_shutdown_signals' src tests docs` should enumerate local ownership.
- `git diff --check` should pass on the unchanged repository.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only planning state.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the current process/session topology no longer reproduces.
- Stop before selecting or creating implementation without the user's lifecycle-policy choice.
- Stop if the selected shape requires a new supervisor, dependency, compatibility promise, or contract not explicitly approved.
- Stop if another active issue owns the same shutdown-policy decision.

## Maintenance Notes

This decision is narrower than same-boot adoption: it applies when Orbit is intentionally shutting down. It is also deeper than Eon's SIGKILL bypass: cooperative Eon shutdown is insufficient if Orbit's accepted cleanup may still strand owned work.
notes: Accepted 2026-08-14: full explicit Session stop forbids survivors. Orbit owns bounded graceful shutdown, Linux per-Session containment escalation, empty verification, and result reporting; Eon only orchestrates. Preserve ORB-C1 and add one explicit shutdown contract in a separate owner-first implementation Bead. macOS remains blocked pending an independently proved containment replacement.
close_reason: Decision accepted: full explicit Session stop forbids survivors; owner-first Linux containment implementation follows in a separate Bead.

comments.text:
Decision evidence and recommendation — awaiting explicit user choice

Current evidence
- Candidate: edge 7c44105e09fc2a5e27f6ae6aee275e58198328fe on Linux 7.0.11-76070011-generic x86_64; target/debug/yazelix-orbit SHA-256 3ee6fa149ed6ac31a2f86acfc928d0b1534376396e92702786fca026c4386128.
- Isolated real-PTY reproduction used Bash job control and a background sleep that ignored HUP and TERM. Before shutdown: Orbit PID 1895292/PPID 1895264/PGID 1895264/SID 1895264; shell PID 1895294/PPID 1895292/PGID 1895294/SID 1895294; background PID 1895296/PPID 1895294/PGID 1895296/SID 1895294; foreground PGID snapshot 1895297. Orbit exited 0 and the shell was gone, but background PID 1895296 remained alive as PPID 1/PGID 1895296/SID 1895294. The harness then sent SIGKILL and verified it gone. No repository file was edited by the reproduction.
- Current owner path remains src/platform.rs:115-134: one initial-group target plus one tcgetpgrp snapshot, HUP then KILL, followed by direct-child kill/wait. The current lifecycle test proves only the initial shell and foreground child. Closed audit orb-audit-orbit-platform-t4s F3 at 750490f40f348b66aa8809c66c40587ca8db741f independently recorded the same survivor class. Eon's separate immediate-SIGKILL gap remains owned by deferred eon-choose-orbit-owned-shutdown-zmn.

Required reference disposition
- POSIX.1-2024 kill and terminal job-control semantics provide process and process-group targets, not a whole-session kill primitive. Negative kill therefore cannot make the current two-group snapshot complete.
- Linux man-pages 6.18 PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER confirms orphan adoption and wait ownership, while proc_tid_children explicitly says live-child enumeration is unreliable unless stopped/frozen. A subreaper plus /proc child traversal is therefore rejected as insufficient proof, even with pidfds; pidfds solve PID reuse, not complete enumeration.
- Linux cgroup v2 documentation provides the needed bounded identity: descendants inherit membership; delegated containment prevents escape; cgroup.kill handles concurrent forks/migrations; cgroup.events populated=0 verifies no live member remains. cgroup.kill is SIGKILL-only, so Orbit must retain a graceful bounded first phase before escalation.
- Process Triage d98c440e13b35fead5ad6b9ed10ed0baf72dc430, especially action/signal.rs and action/executor.rs, supports identity revalidation, staged action, bounded verification, and explicit outcomes. Orbit accepts those mechanics only; it rejects host-wide collection, classification, policy, and /proc scanning.
- FrankenTerm c0e586ff2f161c9426a9230859c355d4bd15ed44 confirms targeted child-tree visibility and staged verification are useful, but its Linux /proc traversal and macOS pgrep traversal are comparison evidence, not complete shutdown authority.
- zmx bea5fe315ca5fcd67f393cef9c8c2b0a6903ebca sends HUP then KILL only to the initial negative PID and waits the direct child; shpool 901e18c3ced010073178b78c0ca2a8cdd43e8581 sends HUP then KILL only to the child PID; abduco 8c32909a159aaa9484c82b71f05b7a73321eb491 exits and unlinks its socket while reaping reported children. These are useful bounded-cleanup comparisons but none proves the distinct-group case, so Orbit must not copy their scope claim.

Compared policy shapes
A. Full explicit Session stop within current PTY/session authority. Result: no distinct job-control group may survive an accepted stop. Current POSIX group/session primitives cannot enumerate and atomically terminate the owned set; a SID or process-name scan has PID-reuse, fork, setsid, and unrelated-process races. The policy is desirable, but this direct implementation shape is rejected. Estimated implementation M-H and correctness risk HIGH; no honest first check can pass without a stronger containment identity.
B. Permitted survivor. Result: Stop means Orbit, the initial group, and one foreground snapshot stop; HUP-ignoring distinct groups may remain under PID 1. Orbit would own the limited targets, deadline, direct-child reap, and honest non-full result; Eon and EonTerm would never compensate. This is approximately S work and LOW implementation risk, but creates surprising resource leaks and makes a successful user-visible Session stop weaker than its name. First check would deliberately assert the survivor. Recommendation: reject.
C. Full stop through platform containment. Result: accepted explicit Session stop forbids every live Orbit-owned descendant from surviving, including distinct process groups and descendants that call setsid. A Linux platform host supplies one delegated, per-Session cgroup before PTY exec; descendants inherit it. Orbit remains outside that kill target and is the sole lifecycle/result owner. Orbit performs its existing graceful PTY/group phase, waits a fixed deadline, uses cgroup.kill only for remaining members, reaps its direct/adopted children, and reports success only after cgroup.events says populated=0. Kernel cgroup membership owns identity/enumeration; the platform seam owns signal mechanics; the Orbit owner loop owns policy, grace/escalation timing, reap/verification coordination, exit result, and error reporting. Eon owns only orchestration. Estimated implementation H and risk HIGH, primarily delegation/launch atomicity, stuck D-state behavior, and packaging availability. This is the recommendation.

Contract, consumer, and portability consequences if C is approved
- Preserve ORB-C1: it still governs survival while Orbit remains running. Add one explicit shutdown contract rather than stretching ORB-C1; allocate its ID only after approval. Success means zero live members by the deadline. Inability to establish containment must fail before PTY spawn; inability to empty/verify it must produce bounded non-success, never a false clean stop.
- Owner-first order: (1) one Orbit implementation/proof bead establishes Linux containment and the new contract; (2) Eon eon-choose-orbit-owned-shutdown-zmn selects cooperative signal-driven shutdown against that exact proof, waits boundedly, and reports failure rather than duplicating PTY cleanup; (3) EonTerm/Venus consumes only Eon's stop result. Pin the exact Orbit proof; no old-version fallback, adapter, or compatibility window. Same-boot adoption remains separate.
- First contract check: start a real job-control shell with an initial group, foreground group, and HUP/TERM-ignoring distinct background group inside the owned containment plus an unrelated sibling outside it; request shutdown; assert Orbit exits success before the deadline, all contained PIDs/groups are gone and membership is empty, the direct child is reaped, and the unrelated sibling remains alive. One forced containment-unavailable case must fail before child spawn.
- Portability: isolated platform dependency. Linux has a credible cgroup-v2 mechanism. Current macOS launchd documentation kills remaining processes only in the job's process group and therefore does not prove distinct-group cleanup; no public, verified per-Session descendant containment plus empty-notification replacement was found. Record this as a macOS blocker with estimated HIGH removal cost and make no macOS runtime claim. Do not weaken the platform-neutral policy to obtain apparent portability.
- Reversal: choose B only if the product intentionally wants explicit Stop to permit orphaned work. Revisit containment only if a smaller kernel/supervisor mechanism proves complete membership, bounded termination, and empty verification without a new daemon or broad scan.

Explicitly rejected in every shape: broad PID/process-name/SID scans as authority, killing a user/system subtree, Eon-owned group discovery or cleanup, unbounded waits, false success after escalation failure, a new daemon, a dependency without a Crate gate, and machine-restart persistence.

Recommended user choice: C — full explicit Session stop, no survivors, implemented owner-first through Linux platform containment. No implementation bead, contract edit, dependency, or code change is authorized or created by this record.

title: Evaluate a Bend2 proof model of Orbit attachment semantics
description:
## Contract routing

This is a bounded research and decision spike for an external proof model. It changes no ORB product contract and does not authorize a Bend2 runtime dependency, production rewrite, generated C/CUDA integration, permanent proof directory, hosted CI job, protocol/schema copy, or change of implementation language. The Rust Orbit implementation and indexed contract proofs remain authoritative.

The first experiment models only the cohesive ORB-C1/ORB-C4/ORB-C7 attachment-and-revision cluster. Selection, terminal semantics, wire encoding, PTY syscalls, graphics, persistence, and Venus are excluded. A successful result may justify a separate user-approved adoption or expansion Bead; it does not widen itself.

Impact: potentially medium if Bend2 expresses a small readable machine-checked lifecycle invariant. Effort: M. Risk: high because Bend2 is unreleased and an external model has an unavoidable refinement gap from Rust. Confidence: medium that the spike can reach a useful adopt/reject decision, low that it should become production infrastructure.

## Current state and evidence

As of 2026-08-11, the public `VictorTaelin/Bend2` repository reports `Bend2 - WIP`, has no commits or license, and cannot supply an inspectable proof language. Do not begin from announcements, private demonstrations, Bend1, or inferred syntax. Begin only from a public exact Bend2 release or commit with source, license, proof semantics, documentation, and a reproducible toolchain.

Orbit evidence:

- `docs/CONTRACTS.md` defines ORB-C1 client-independent PTY lifetime, ORB-C4 complete-frame attachment plus strictly ordered revisions, and ORB-C7 bounded slow/broken-client behavior.
- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:338-367` owns strict complete-frame revision reduction.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:562-598` owns bounded role-specific attachment framing before payload buffering.
- `src/main.rs:236+` keeps the authoritative revision in the single owner loop.
- `src/main.rs:1061-1075` owns checked revision advance and detach-side selection cleanup.
- `tests/lifecycle.rs` and `src/presentation.rs` provide the executable real-PTY traces that any abstract model must map to without replacing.

## Prerequisites

- This Bead remains deferred until the user selects it and Bend2 satisfies the public-source gate. Model the current accepted post-ORBS-v3 proof at `6de95296d252c119d4fdba2d9b03cec1a09355ae`; closed `orb-ll1.1` is historical provenance, not an active blocker.
- Bend2 must have an inspectable public source revision or release, an explicit license compatible with this research use, official language/proof documentation, a reproducible Linux toolchain, and a way to verify proofs non-interactively.
- Do not start while another issue or agent changes the selected Orbit state-transition surface.

The Kani and Verus evaluation Beads are comparison evidence only and are not sequencing dependencies.

## Required references before model code

Required: current `AGENTS.md`; exact accepted ORB-C1, ORB-C4, and ORB-C7 proofs; the complete accepted owner-loop attachment/detach/frame/pressure paths and their real-PTY tests; `docs/CRATES.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md`, and `docs/RATIONALE.md`; exact public Bend2 source, license, compiler/runtime, proof checker, trust model, totality/consistency claims, numeric and linear/resource semantics, FFI/extraction behavior, supported platforms, and official examples at one immutable identity.

Comparison only: the sibling Kani and Verus spikes, Lean/Agda-style external models, and Bend1/HVM history. Rejected: treating creator claims as proof semantics, importing Bend1 behavior, or copying Orbit Rust into a second executable implementation.

If repository production code, tests, manifests, docs, generated files, or configuration would be edited, first claim this non-epic Bead, record the execution baseline, and pass the evidence-first gate. Any tool/dependency or manifest change requires the full crate/dependency gate and user approval. Hosted automation requires a separately justified CI contract.

## Smallest model

Define a finite, explicit transition system independent of terminal cell contents:

- State: PTY/session liveness, zero-or-one attached client, authoritative revision, whether the attachment's initial complete frame has been emitted, and bounded client-output disposition.
- Events: attach attempt, complete initial frame, authoritative frame publication, client detach/failure, output pressure, PTY close, and shutdown.
- Observations: attachment outcome, complete-frame revision, disconnect/failure, and PTY/session liveness.

Prove only:

1. At most one client owns attachment in every reachable state.
2. Client detach/failure never changes a live PTY/session to dead.
3. A successful attachment cannot expose a later revision before its coherent initial complete frame.
4. Every later exposed frame revision is strictly greater than the previously exposed revision.
5. Bounded client-output pressure disconnects/fails that client without creating a second attachment or unbounded modeled history.

Use the smallest numeric domain sufficient to expose ordering mistakes, then state exactly whether Bend2 proves the invariant generically or only for the finite bound. Include one intentionally invalid transition or inverted theorem and demonstrate that Bend2 rejects it.

Do not model ORBF/ORBS bytes, terminal cells, libghostty, PTY/syscall behavior, selection, effects, viewport, search, graphics, persistence, multiple sessions, multiple clients, remote transport, Eon/Venus policy, or performance.

## Method and decision

1. Pin the exact accepted Orbit subject and exact Bend2 identity.
2. Record Bend2's trusted computing base, proof-checking semantics, consistency/termination boundaries, axioms/unsafe escapes, numeric semantics, and whether executable evaluation can diverge from proofs.

title: Enforce truthful ORBF v1 capabilities
description:
## Contract routing

Hardens `ORB-C6` and preserves `ORB-C4` plus `ORB-C3`, `ORB-C5`, and `ORB-C7` through `ORB-C11`. This does not add a capability, change the accepted ORBF v1 producer values, or authorize a new wire revision.

Consumer: Orbit's authoritative presentation producer and every canonical `orbit-protocol` ORBF v1 decoder, including Venus.

Trigger: code encodes or decodes an ORBF v1 complete frame.

Result: the canonical owner accepts only capability values truthful for accepted ORBF v1: hyperlink support is advertised and Kitty graphics are declared unsupported. A contradictory capability combination fails before the frame is accepted by a reducer or consumer.

Important failures: no partial frame acceptance, no silent normalization, no second validator in Orbit or Venus, and no future-graphics semantics folded into v1.

## Why

The accepted ORB-C6 contract says ORBF v1 advertises hyperlinks and explicitly leaves Kitty graphics unsupported, but the shared codec currently accepts every boolean combination. This lets structurally canonical bytes contradict the capability contract at its trust boundary.

Impact: MED. Effort: S. Risk: MED because decoder hardening must be classified against published bytes. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:130-135`: `Capabilities` exposes independent hyperlink and Kitty booleans.
- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:375-388`: `encode_frame` writes either combination after shape validation.
- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:425-451`: `decode_frame` accepts either canonical boolean.
- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:549-578`: `validate_frame` does not validate capability semantics.
- `src/presentation.rs:134-146`: the sole accepted producer always emits `hyperlinks: true` and `kitty_graphics: false`.
- `README.md:97-101` and `docs/CONTRACTS.md:34`: accepted ORBF v1 behavior advertises hyperlinks and declares Kitty unsupported.
- Audit `orb-audit-orbit-protocols-bkk` reproduced and recorded the gap at Orbit `7d34399b15496513f7f91b94acd32e8d04389e16`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a co-located protocol test, construct an otherwise valid ORBF v1 frame.
2. Set `kitty_graphics: true`; observe that `encode_frame` and `decode_frame` both succeed.
3. Set `hyperlinks: false` on an otherwise accepted rich frame; observe that both paths also succeed.

Expected from the indexed ORB-C6 contract: ORBF v1 rejects capability values that contradict its advertised hyperlink support and explicit lack of Kitty graphics. Actual at the audited revision: both booleans are treated as unconstrained canonical data.

## Reference classification

Required before code:

- Current `AGENTS.md`, this complete Bead, `docs/CONTRACTS.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md`, `docs/RATIONALE.md`, and `docs/CRATES.md`.
- Exact accepted ORB-C6 proof and the `orb-bi4.3` / `orb-bi4.9` evidence that selected the capability representation and canonical codec.
- Exact Orbit producer call site and exact Venus `orbit-protocol` pin/decoder at the execution baseline.

Comparison only:

- Deferred graphics epic `orb-j2i`; it owns a future ORBF/ORBS revision and must not redefine current v1 validation.

Rejected scope:

- A feature probe, compatibility adapter, second validator, serializer, graphics resource plane, or dependency.

Record the Execution baseline and pre-implementation Reference gate before the first test or production edit. No Crate gate is expected because no manifest or dependency change is authorized.

## Scope

In scope:

- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs` capability validation and focused co-located tests.
- `README.md` LOC scorecard if Rust LOC changes.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md` proof lifecycle metadata for hardened ORB-C6.
- The minimum accepted-proof metadata required by repository policy.

Out of scope:

- Changing the accepted producer values in `src/presentation.rs`.
- Editing Venus, ORBS session messages, graphics behavior, capability negotiation, or a wire version.
- Broad codec cleanup, fuzzing, formal proof, or new dependencies.

## Implementation notes

1. Use TDD: first prove encode and decode currently accept `kitty_graphics: true`, and `hyperlinks: false` under ORBF v1.
2. Put the invariant in the existing shared frame-validation owner so encode and decode cannot drift.
3. Reject invalid values explicitly; do not coerce them.
4. Confirm every accepted producer/test fixture uses the selected v1 values and adjust only fixtures that were accidentally contract-invalid.
5. Classify the result as compatible hardening of contract-invalid bytes. If any accepted producer or known consumer relies on another combination, stop for a user compatibility decision instead of changing v1.
6. Follow the proof lifecycle: run indexed ORB-C6 checks, create the proof-bearing commit while the Bead remains open, then update the exact proof revision and closure metadata as required.

Portability disposition: neutral.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A focused encoder test rejects ORBF v1 with `hyperlinks: false` or `kitty_graphics: true`.
2. A focused decoder test rejects bytes carrying either contract-invalid value before `FrameReducer` acceptance.
3. Valid rich frames remain byte-for-byte identical and the exact Orbit producer still emits `true/false`.
4. Venus needs no compensating validator or schema change.
5. No ORBS bytes, direct dependency, compatibility window, feature probe, or future graphics behavior is added.
6. ORB-C6 is recorded as hardened at an exact accepted proof revision; other affected proved contracts are preserved and their indexed checks are rerun or honestly downgraded.
7. README Rust LOC and proof metadata are current at closure.

## Verification

- `cargo test --locked -p orbit-protocol` should pass the focused invalid-capability and existing canonical codec checks.
- `cargo fmt --all --check` should exit 0.
- `cargo check --locked --workspace` should exit 0.
- `cargo test --locked --workspace` should exit 0.
- `cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .` should report `governance: ok`.
- `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` should exit 0.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0.
- Run the indexed ORB-C6 checks named by `docs/CONTRACTS.md`.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue before closure.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the accepted ORBF v1 contract does not uniquely require hyperlink support on and Kitty graphics off.
- Stop if any exact accepted producer or known consumer emits or relies on another combination.
- Stop if the fix requires a new wire revision, product capability, cross-repository edit, manifest change, or dependency.
- Stop if another active issue owns the protocol validation surface.

## Maintenance notes

Keep one invariant owner. Do not add per-consumer guards. Future graphics work replaces the protocol revision under `orb-j2i`; it does not justify making current v1 capability bytes ambiguous.

title: Hold ORBS presentation during synchronized terminal output
description:
## Contract routing

Harden proved ORB-C4 coherent complete-frame publication and ORB-C6 rich terminal presentation. Preserve ORB-C1 through ORB-C3, ORB-C5, ORB-C7 through ORB-C11, canonical ORBS v3, and all ordered effect behavior. No new wire value or product contract is proposed.

Consumer: an attached ORBS client such as Venus.

Trigger: authoritative libghostty terminal state enters DEC private mode 2026 synchronized output while PTY bytes continue arriving across one or more reads.

Result: Orbit continues parsing every byte, updating authoritative terminal state, sending terminal replies, and preserving ordered effects, but does not publish intermediate coalescible presentation frames while synchronized output is active. When the mode ends, Orbit publishes exactly the latest complete state at one newer revision. A bounded timeout releases a producer that forgets the end marker and publishes the latest state rather than freezing presentation indefinitely.

Important failures: attachment, resize, terminal exit, client loss, clipboard effects, output pressure, and a missing end marker remain bounded. Orbit must not infer application frames from PTY write size, read size, silence, flush calls, row order, or process identity.

## Why and evidence

The user observed direct Nova welcome animation flicker that worsens toward lower rows, while the same `yzx screen` animation is stable inside Zellij.

- Current inspected Orbit identity: `a119bd5e6838c39cf05e273eb1a5c778ddc39f00`.
- `src/main.rs:354-365` publishes a frame after every PTY read that changes terminal state.
- `src/main.rs:1070-1083` bounds each read to 8192 bytes. A large top-to-bottom redraw can therefore become multiple visible ORBS revisions.
- The selected libghostty-vt 0.2.1 exposes authoritative `Terminal::mode(Mode::SYNC_OUTPUT)`; Orbit currently never consults it.
- Pinned Ghostty `a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083` suppresses rendering while synchronized output is active and resets a stuck producer after 1000 ms.
- Nova Zellij emits DEC 2026 around its outer render when supported, but its differential output is also smaller than Anima's full-screen redraw. The user's comparison therefore supports the diagnosis without by itself proving which mechanism avoided every partial read.
- Required producer companion: Anima `yzs-emit-synchronized-frames-2tg`.

Impact: MED for visible animation/TUI tearing and correctness of the standard terminal mode. Effort: M. Risk: MED because initial attachment, timeout, effects, and output pressure intersect the owner loop. Confidence: HIGH that Orbit lacks mode enforcement; MED that this alone explains every observed Zellij difference.

## Scope

In scope:
- The authoritative PTY/read/publication path in `src/main.rs`.
- Existing libghostty mode inspection and the existing 100 ms owner-loop wakeup.
- Focused deterministic and real-PTY tests for split begin/payload/end input, timeout, attachment, exit, and pressure.
- ORB-C4/ORB-C6 proof metadata, changelog if accepted as user-visible behavior, and LOC accounting.

Out of scope:
- ORBS changes, a new event type, raw escape parsing outside libghostty, a second terminal model, application detection, read-buffer enlargement as the fix, arbitrary frame-rate throttling, Venus changes, Anima changes, or a new dependency.

## Reference classification

Required before code: current issue and contracts; complete PTY owner loop, output queue, negotiation, effects, and tests; exact libghostty-vt 0.2.1 `Mode::SYNC_OUTPUT` behavior; Ghostty `a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083` synchronized-render suppression and one-second reset; DEC 2026 semantics from a maintained primary terminal reference.

Comparison only: crossterm 0.28.1 producer API and Nova Zellij's synchronized outer-render path.

Rejected: PTY packet assumptions, drain-until-EAGAIN as an atomicity guarantee, larger reads, sleeps after output, frame-rate caps, copying Ghostty's renderer/thread, and protocol markers sent to Venus.

## Implementation notes

Use libghostty's authoritative mode value after each applied PTY chunk. Track only the minimum pending-presentation state and one bounded deadline in the existing owner loop. Continue ordered clipboard publication under its current ORB-C11 ordering; withhold only coalescible frames. On normal end, publish one latest frame. On the accepted timeout, clear the libghostty mode through its existing setter and publish once.

Define initial attachment during an active synchronized update explicitly: do not send a partial initial frame. Complete attachment with the last stable state if already retained, or defer the initial frame until normal end/timeout using the smallest existing state shape. Preserve the one-client negotiation bound.

## Acceptance

1. A begin marker split from payload and end across several reads yields no intermediate ORBS frame and exactly one final frame with all rows.
2. Begin/payload/end in one read still yields one ordinary final revision.
3. Ordinary output outside mode 2026 preserves current prompt publication and revision ordering.
4. A producer that never ends is released at the accepted one-second bound, the mode is cleared, and latest state is published once; subsequent output remains live.
5. A client attaching during synchronized output never receives a partial initial frame and cannot remain blocked past the same bound.
6. Clipboard effects, terminal replies, semantic input, resize, client loss, PTY exit, selection invalidation, and bounded output pressure preserve their existing owners and ordering.
7. Detached processing accumulates no frame history; reattachment receives one latest coherent state.
8. The companion Anima producer plus Eonova rollout shows no top-to-bottom welcome flicker. This issue itself does not claim native Venus acceptance.
9. No dependency, wire revision, renderer change, or application-specific rule is added.

## Verification

- Focused deterministic owner-loop tests for mode transitions, timeout, attach, effect ordering, and pressure
- A real PTY corpus whose synchronized payload exceeds 8192 bytes
- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo check --locked`
- `cargo test --locked`
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .`
- `git diff --check`

## Stop conditions

Stop for explicit user approval if evidence requires a new ORB-C contract, ORBS change, dependency, public timeout setting, or second retained presentation model. Stop if libghostty does not expose enough authoritative mode control; prefer a small upstream binding correction over raw escape parsing. Stop if another active issue owns the same PTY publication surface.

Chosen ownership and code shape:

- Client owns only whether its first complete frame is still owed after Hello.
- libghostty Mode::SYNC_OUTPUT remains authoritative. Orbit continues PTY parsing, terminal replies, clipboard effects, semantic input, selection invalidation, resize, detach, pressure handling, and exit processing while withholding only frames.
- The first changed PTY turn advances once; later held PTY turns coalesce into that revision. Normal end or a one-second std::time watchdog publishes the latest complete state. Timeout clears the authoritative mode first; exit releases immediately.

title: Prove host-owned history, native scrolling, selection, and copy
description:
Planning container for the minimum useful native-terminal history baseline before Eon dogfood and graduation.

Ownership:
- Orbit and its sole libghostty terminal own retained history, the authoritative viewport, active selection, and copied text.
- Venus owns native gesture capture, display and accessibility from the current complete ORBF frame, explicit copy action, and the native clipboard side effect.
- Venus has no history page cache, stable row tokens, row-anchor table, snapshot mirror, or second terminal/history model.

Contract routing:
- orb-j0m.2 is complete. ORB-C8 is proved at 840a67c0cb32b334ed54888321d5ca77e58117b0 and preserves ORB-C1 through ORB-C7.
- orb-j0m.3 is complete. ORB-C9 is proved at 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757 and preserves ORB-C1 through ORB-C8.
- ORB-C9 deliberately replaces ORBS v1 with ORBS v2. The accepted owner-first breaking order is Orbit proof, Venus ven-4sn consumer update, then orb-j0m.4 acceptance; there is no adapter, dual support, feature probe, or compatibility window.
- orb-j0m.5 changes no product contract and runs one direct Valgrind Memcheck lifecycle against the exact accepted selection-capable Orbit revision.
- orb-j0m.4 is the no-code cross-repository acceptance gate after the Orbit owner, Valgrind hardening, and Venus consumer proofs.
- Complete ordered ORBF frames remain the only structured presentation and resynchronization authority. Search remains separate in orb-qcc.

This epic is a planning container. It must not be claimed for production code, tests, manifests, protocol edits, or contract-index edits.
design:
Run after the closed orb-bi4.5 visible-state hardening gate.

Execute one frontier at a time:

2. orb-j0m.2 is complete: Orbit routes existing ORBS v1 wheel and key input from authoritative modes, drives the libghostty viewport, and publishes complete frames under ORB-C8.
