Reuse the accepted owner loop and libghostty-vt 0.2.1. The required surfaces already exist: Terminal.scroll_viewport, authoritative mouse state, current-viewport GridRef resolution, Selection snapshots, Terminal.set_selection, bounded Terminal.format_selection_buf, and render-state selected-cell projection.

ORB-C8 is the viewport source of truth: client loss preserves the current Orbit-owned viewport and reattachment starts from that view. title: Choose the libghostty-native interaction boundary
description:
Decision: GO for a direct libghostty-native viewport and selection boundary. This decision changes no runtime contract and preserves ORB-C1 through ORB-C7.

Orbit keeps its existing sole libghostty terminal authority. Venus sends bounded semantic viewport and selection gestures; Orbit mutates the authoritative libghostty viewport or selection and publishes a newer complete ORBF frame. Copy text is formatted by Orbit from the terminal-owned selection and only the bounded result crosses to Venus for an explicit native clipboard action.

This is not a go for history paging. No stable row identity, epoch, anchor, retained-row page, client cache, snapshot, raw-byte parser, local fork, private adapter, or upstream change is required.
design:
Accepted public mechanisms in libghostty-vt 0.2.1:
- Terminal.scroll_viewport supports Top, Bottom, bounded Delta, and absolute Row behavior.
- Terminal.is_mouse_tracking exposes authoritative application-mouse ownership.
- Viewport grid references resolve current visible cells without long-lived external identity.
- Selection gesture APIs translate bounded press, drag, and release input into terminal selections.
- Terminal.set_selection and RenderState selected-cell data make ORBF selected styling authoritative.
- Terminal.format_selection_buf supports bounded terminal-owned plain-text extraction.

Accepted boundary:
1. Orbit decides wheel or viewport behavior from current terminal modes and owns the native viewport mutation.
2. Every accepted viewport or selection mutation produces a complete ordered ORBF frame; Venus never materializes retained history separately.
3. Selection coordinates are valid only against the current viewport and current interaction. They are not durable history identifiers.
4. A terminal mutation during an active drag cancels and resets the gesture. Successful release freezes bounded copy text immediately. Later ordinary output clears potentially remapped visual selection but may retain that immutable copy candidate until explicit copy, a new selection, resize or reflow, screen transition, detach, client loss, or exit.
5. Detach or client loss returns the viewport to Bottom and clears transient interaction state before reattachment.
6. Application mouse tracking keeps normal mouse gestures application-owned. Venus may expose a separate explicit host-selection gesture, but its native modifier policy remains consumer-owned.

Rejected boundary:
The prior history request and response plane, page tokens, row offsets, cache epochs, client page cache, stale-page recovery, and snapshot identity are deleted from the plan. The tracked-reference erase defect remains valid evidence but is irrelevant to this short-lived viewport interaction. orb-upstream-libghostty-reference-loss-dck preserves it independently.

Portability disposition: neutral terminal and protocol behavior above the existing isolated Linux platform seam. No crate change is selected.
acceptance_criteria:
1. GO: the accepted baseline uses libghostty native viewport, selection, selected-cell rendering, and selection formatting through Orbit authority.
2. ORB-C1 through ORB-C7 remain unchanged by this planning decision.
3. Complete ordered ORBF frames remain the only live presentation and reattachment authority.
4. No long-lived history identity or retained-row model crosses the Orbit and Venus boundary.
5. Application mouse tracking is decided by Orbit from authoritative terminal state; Venus does not infer terminal modes from rendered text.
6. Selection endpoints are bounded current-viewport coordinates. Mutation, resize or reflow, screen transition, detach, client loss, and exit have explicit clearing or cancellation semantics before implementation.
7. Copy text is formatted and bounded by Orbit; Venus owns only explicit user action and the native clipboard side effect.
8. orb-j0m.2 and orb-j0m.3 must index their exact user-approved contracts before production code and classify any ORBS change and Venus update order.
9. The simple complete-frame path is measured before any coalescing, paging, caching, patching, or dependency is considered.
10. orb-upstream-libghostty-reference-loss-dck is P3 deferred and is not a prerequisite.
11. No production, test, manifest, generated, protocol, contract-index, Venus, or Eon file changed in this decision.
notes:
The earlier NO-GO remains correct for client-materialized history pages: erased tracked references can silently remap under the pinned dependency. The user chose not to make that API part of the product boundary.

The new design avoids the failed identity requirement instead of compensating for it. It uses dependency-owned viewport and selection state already present in the accepted crate and keeps one complete presentation owner.
close_reason: User accepted the direct libghostty-native interaction boundary; stable history identity is not required.

title: Drive the authoritative libghostty viewport
description:
Orbit implementation child for the authoritative native history viewport.

Contract routing:
- Proposes this exact new native-viewport contract for explicit user approval: On a healthy attachment, Orbit routes each vertical-wheel message from authoritative libghostty state. Active mouse tracking sends only mouse input to the PTY; otherwise an active alternate screen with DEC private mode 1007 sends only terminal-aware cursor input; otherwise Orbit applies one row of native viewport movement. Primary movement clamps within retained history and no-history movement is an accepted no-op. Every host-owned wheel action queues Accepted followed by a strictly newer complete frame of the resulting authoritative viewport. A successful semantic key event that emits PTY bytes returns a scrolled primary viewport to the live area and queues its resulting complete frame. Client disconnection does not transfer, reconstruct, or reset viewport ownership; reattachment begins with one coherent frame of the current Orbit-owned viewport. Rejected or malformed input cannot mutate terminal state, and viewport interaction cannot block authoritative PTY processing.
- Creates and indexes that contract only after the user approves the wording; planning alone changes no contract.
- Preserves and reruns ORB-C1 through ORB-C7, especially ORB-C2 terminal authority, ORB-C4 complete ordered frames, ORB-C5 semantic input, and ORB-C7 pressure.
- Changes no ORBS or ORBF bytes and no orbit-protocol API. The known Venus consumer at c905bf9610581747f1b07565814b501ca66cfaa6 already emits the required bounded Mouse and Key values, so the Orbit runtime may land first with no schema compatibility window or consumer adapter.

User-visible behavior:
The existing vertical wheel scrolls retained primary history, routes to mouse-aware applications, or follows DEC 1007 alternate-scroll behavior according to Orbit authoritative state. Scrolling down or typing terminal-producing input returns to live output. Orbit keeps the current viewport across a transient Venus disconnect and sends that coherent current view on reattachment. Venus stores no history pages, anchors, epochs, or terminal modes.
design:
Prerequisites and evidence:
orb-j0m.1 is closed. Before code, claim this Bead, record the Execution baseline, index the user-approved contract, and pass the Reference gate.
- Required before code: libghostty-vt 0.2.1 public Terminal, Screen, Mode, MouseEncoder, KeyEncoder, ScrollViewport, and Scrollbar APIs; pinned Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083 Surface.scrollCallback, Terminal.scrollViewport, PageList.scroll and scrollbar, screen switching, and key scroll-to-bottom behavior; official XTerm Control Sequences Patch 410 behavior for DEC private mode 1007.
- Comparison only: current Ghostty scroll-to-bottom and scroll action documentation.
- Rejected scope: WezTerm-style history pages or client row caches, Mosh-style history replication, and the superseded Orbit paging design.
No crate gate is expected: the standard owner loop and selected libghostty dependency expose every required mechanism.

Smallest implementation shape:
1. Keep canonical ORBS v1 unchanged. Reuse Mouse buttons Four and Five for one-row vertical wheel actions and reuse successful Key input as the native return-live trigger. Do not add Viewport, Delta, Top, Bottom, ReturnLive, page, anchor, epoch, or cache messages.
2. 3. title: Drive authoritative selection and copy in the native viewport
description: Accepted Orbit implementation for ORB-C9 authoritative current-viewport selection and bounded copy. ORBS v2 carries revision-bound Begin, ordered Update and Finish, explicit Copy, and bounded CopiedText. Orbit owns selection resolution, selected presentation, and immutable frozen text; Venus remains responsible for pointer gesture policy, accessibility from canonical frames, and the native clipboard side effect. The breaking Orbit-first update is accepted at 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757: Venus updates separately through ven-4sn, with no v1 adapter, dual support, feature probe, or compatibility window. ORB-C1 through ORB-C9 are proved at that exact revision.
design: Accepted implementation shape: the existing owner loop keeps one active anchor cell, one frozen String candidate, and whether libghostty currently presents a selection. Begin validates the exact latest frame revision and current-viewport coordinate; Update and Finish require the uninterrupted active phase. Every accepted phase resolves fresh Point::Viewport GridRefs, creates one linear libghostty Selection, reserves worst-case Accepted-plus-frame output, installs the terminal-owned selection, and publishes one newer complete frame. Finish probes libghostty plain, unwrap, and trim formatting for its required length, enforces the 1 MiB copy limit before exact allocation, then freezes the whole UTF-8 result before committing state. Copy returns only that immutable client-scoped candidate. Every non-selection terminal mutation clears the active anchor and visual selection before mutation. PTY output, viewport movement, resize or reflow, and active-screen transitions preserve the frozen value because they cannot reinterpret it. A newer valid Begin, client loss, or exit clears it. ORBS v2 and ORBF v1 remain platform-neutral above the existing Linux seam. No new module, crate, manifest feature, tracked endpoint, Gesture object, pixel protocol, request table, page cache, upstream change, or clipboard owner is added.
acceptance_criteria:
1. ORB-C9 is user-approved and indexed before production code with Orbit as selection, styling, and text owner and Venus as gesture-policy, accessibility, and clipboard owner.
2. ORBS v2 remains the approved breaking Orbit-first replacement, names Venus at c905bf9610581747f1b07565814b501ca66cfaa6, and has no adapter, dual support, probe, or compatibility window.
3. Begin binds to the exact latest complete-frame revision and a valid current-viewport cell; rejected input cannot mutate interaction or copy state.
4. Begin and Update use fresh libghostty viewport GridRefs and linear Selection snapshots, install the sole terminal-owned selection, and queue Accepted followed by a newer complete frame.
5. Finish formats its fresh snapshot with libghostty plain, unwrap, and trim semantics, enforces the 1 MiB bound, atomically installs the final selection and whole immutable String, then queues Accepted followed by a newer complete frame. Failure exposes no partial text.
6. Exact text is correct for forward, reverse, single-cell, wrapping, hard breaks, combining and wide graphemes, empty and erased cells, and retained rows visible in the current viewport.
7. Every non-selection terminal mutation cancels an active interaction and clears visual selection before mutation. Successfully frozen text survives later PTY output, viewport movement, resize or reflow, and active-screen transitions without reinterpretation.
8. A newer valid Begin, detach or client loss, and exit clear interaction, visual selection, and frozen text without resetting the ORB-C8 viewport. Reattachment starts from that view without stale client-scoped selection state.
9. Coordinates, revision, span, formatted bytes, per-event work, storage, payloads, input, and queued output remain explicitly bounded and cannot block PTY processing or cleanup.
10. One strong codec check and one real-terminal lifecycle check cover revision binding, Unicode text, bounds, phase order, terminal-mutation clearing, immutable retention through ordinary output, alternate screen and resize, pressure, detach and reattach, client loss, and response ordering.
11. Closure records exact Orbit proof, ORB-C1 through ORB-C9 disposition, compatibility order, dependency footprint, portability, LOC, measurements, and deferred autoscroll, word or line selection, search, clipboard effects, graphics, and restart gaps.

Scope boundary: Orbit current-viewport linear cell selection and bounded plain-text copy only. title: Accept native history, scrolling, selection, and copy
description:
Final no-code cross-repository acceptance child for the native history baseline. It changes no runtime contract.

Start only after orb-j0m.5 completes its one-scenario Valgrind Memcheck hardening check against the accepted selection-capable Orbit revision and Venus ven-4sn proves its consumer against ORB-C8 at 840a67c0cb32b334ed54888321d5ca77e58117b0 and ORB-C9 at 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757. Venus is already re-primed away from the discarded page-cache design. Use the real Orbit and Venus pair; a diagnostic client, recorded frame, replay source, or Memcheck scenario cannot substitute for native interaction.

Dogfood ordinary shell output, long retained primary history, rapid wheel movement, byte-producing key return to live, wrapped Unicode and wide graphemes, current-viewport selection and copy, alternate-screen Neovim and Yazi, application mouse mode, DEC 1007 alternate scroll, resize and reflow, pruning, CSI 3 J, detach, reattach, client loss, mutation during selection, output after Finish, oversized copy, and stopped-reader pressure. Record exact revisions, environment, user-visible behavior, bounds, latency, memory, accessibility, and failure ownership.
design:
Acceptance compares the simple native-owner path with ordinary terminal behavior, not with the discarded paging architecture.

Use the exact accepted complete-frame queue and one-client boundary. ORB-C8 is already fixed: active mouse tracking sends only application mouse input; alternate screen with DEC 1007 sends only terminal-aware cursor input; all other vertical wheel input is host-owned one-row viewport movement, including an accepted no-op frame when alternate-screen history cannot move. A byte-producing key returns a scrolled primary viewport to live. Disconnect preserves the Orbit-owned viewport; reattachment projects that view.

Observe whether one local gesture round trip plus a complete frame is responsive enough. A performance miss is recorded with its smallest owner and measurement; this Bead does not authorize coalescing, patches, caching, protocol redesign, or implementation.

The accepted initial selection ceiling is current-viewport linear cells. Rectangle selection, drag autoscroll, word or line click selection, auto-copy, rich clipboard formats, and retained-history search are later choices rather than acceptance blockers.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Exact Orbit and Venus proof revisions, ORB-C and VEN-C IDs, compatibility order, commands, environment, and known limitations are recorded before dogfood. Orbit includes ORB-C8 at 840a67c0cb32b334ed54888321d5ca77e58117b0, ORB-C9 and ORBS v2 at 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757, and the exact orb-j0m.5 manual Memcheck result for that selection-capable revision.
2. Primary-screen host scrolling traverses authoritative retained history and clamps or returns to live without PTY wheel bytes, stale rows, duplicated presentation, paging state, or client-owned history. A successful byte-producing key returns a scrolled primary viewport to live.
3. Active application mouse tracking is coherent in Neovim and Yazi: wheel input reaches the application and does not also move or frame a host viewport.
4. On the alternate screen without application mouse tracking, DEC 1007 enabled sends only terminal-aware cursor input; DEC 1007 disabled performs the accepted host-owned no-op and publishes its newer complete frame. Neither path invents client-owned history.
5. Output while scrolled, pruning, CSI 3 J, resize and reflow preserve one libghostty-owned viewport and complete-frame convergence. Disconnect does not reset or transfer viewport ownership; reattachment begins with the current Orbit-owned view.
6. Cell-granular selection and explicit copy return exact authoritative plain text across current and stale start revisions, forward and reverse drags, wrapping, hard breaks, Unicode, combining and wide graphemes, and retained rows visible in the viewport.
7. A non-selection mutation during an active selection cancels cleanly. After Finish, terminal output, resize or reflow, and active-screen transitions clear stale visual selection without changing the frozen copy candidate. A newer valid Begin, client loss, or exit clears that candidate without resetting the ORB-C8 viewport.
8. Gesture-to-frame and copy latency, full-frame and copy bytes, CPU, memory, input work, queued output, and stopped-reader behavior are measured under rapid interaction and long output. Measurements do not become broader performance claims, and the single Memcheck scenario does not become a general memory-safety claim.
9. Accessibility exposes the accepted viewport, authoritative selected styling, copy result or failure, and reconnect state from the same frame and interaction results used visually.
10. Every confirmed defect is assigned to exactly one Orbit or Venus owner with the exact compatibility sequence. No product code, test, manifest, adapter, dependency, trace format, page cache, or upstream change is made here.
11. The result records one outcome: accepted for Eon dogfood, or orb-j0m remains open with one named owner gap. Search and deferred selection enhancements cannot block this result.
12. Parent orb-j0m reconciles owner and consumer proofs, contracts, Memcheck evidence, measurements, portability, LOC, and remaining search, semantic-region, effects, graphics, restart, multi-session, and remote limitations before closure.

Scope boundary:
No implementation. No search, semantic regions, agent observer, effects, graphics, patch protocol, page cache, workspace, distribution, multiple sessions, remote transport, or restart persistence.
notes:
Venus ven-4sn is re-primed against the accepted host-owned viewport, history, selection, and copy boundary at 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757. It keeps no page cache, epoch, stable anchor, row token, or client-owned terminal selection. It remains deferred until orb-j0m.5 closes, then becomes the next implementation frontier.

orb-j0m.5 is an Orbit-only P2 hardening prerequisite after the selection proof and before this acceptance. Its one direct Memcheck lifecycle checks the integrated Rust, libghostty, libc, process, and descriptor seam; it does not replace real Venus interaction, accessibility, performance measurement, or dogfood.

The deferred upstream tracked-reference correction is independent and absent from the acceptance prerequisites.

title: Prove one Orbit lifecycle under Valgrind Memcheck
description:
Repository-hardening slice with no new user-visible behavior or product contract. After the accepted ORB-C9 selection proof, run one deterministic real Orbit server lifecycle under Valgrind Memcheck across the Rust, libghostty C ABI and Zig implementation, and direct libc PTY and socket seam.

The scenario starts one actual Orbit server and child process, attaches a protocol-faithful client, drives representative VT output, resizes, scrolls, selects and copies, detaches, reattaches, and exits the child and server cleanly. It checks memory access, initialization, deallocation, heap retention, and file-descriptor lifecycle at the integrated boundary that ordinary Rust checks cannot observe.

Contract routing:
- Changes no product contract, wire behavior, runtime policy, dependency, supported platform, or proof status by itself.
- Hardens the exact accepted implementation surfaces supporting ORB-C1, ORB-C2, ORB-C4 through ORB-C9. Reconfirm the accepted IDs and proof revisions at activation.
- Runs after orb-j0m.3 and before orb-j0m.4 cross-repository acceptance, so the exact selection-capable Orbit revision is checked before dogfood.

Scope:
- One Linux-only deterministic end-to-end lifecycle and one direct Valgrind Memcheck invocation.
- The exact pinned libghostty-vt and libghostty-vt-sys build, underlying Ghostty revision, Rust toolchain, Zig toolchain, Valgrind version, optimization/debug-info mode, command, suppressions, elapsed time, and result.
- Fatal memory errors, definite or indirect leaks, and leaked or invalid file descriptors.
- Non-fatal reporting and classification of possibly lost and still-reachable allocations.
- The smallest reusable local command or script only if direct invocation cannot remain reproducible without it.

Out of scope:
- Running the complete Cargo suite under Valgrind, per-push or scheduled CI, a CI matrix, macOS Valgrind support, cargo-valgrind or another wrapper dependency, ASan or Miri implementation, performance claims, fuzzing, coverage, product changes, a test-only product mode, a new binary, or broad suppression import.
design:
## Implementation plan

1. Start only after orb-j0m.3 closes with an accepted proof-bearing revision. Re-read the exact ORB-C1 through ORB-C9 index and record an Execution baseline for this one hardening issue before any tracked test, script, suppression, workflow, Nix, or documentation edit.
2. Pass the Reference gate before edits. Required primary evidence: the exact Valgrind Memcheck and core-option manuals; the exact pinned libghostty-vt, libghostty-vt-sys, and Ghostty sources exercised by the scenario; and the current Orbit lifecycle harness and unsafe platform seam. Inspect Ghostty Valgrind and suppression mechanisms only if the first unsuppressed run reports an upstream or runtime-owned finding. Record the exact selected tool and source identities plus relevant licenses.
3. Keep the user-selected tool shape: invoke the Valgrind executable directly. Prefer an already supplied system or Nix tool and add no Cargo wrapper, Rust dependency, framework, product binary, or installation automation. Stop for user choice before adding hosted CI, a Nix package surface, installer logic, or another dynamic-analysis tool.
4. Build the exact accepted Orbit and pinned libghostty artifacts with useful debug symbols. Record optimization mode and prove that the actual yazelix-orbit server process, not only Cargo or the test harness, runs under Memcheck. Prefer direct server wrapping; use narrowly scoped child tracing only if necessary and prevent unrelated shells or helpers from contaminating the result.
5. Reuse the existing protocol and lifecycle helpers where possible. Drive one bounded scenario through server start, real child PTY output with representative VT state, client attach, resize, host viewport scroll, authoritative selection and copy, detach, reattach, child exit, server exit, socket cleanup, and process reaping. Do not run unrelated tests.
6. Use the smallest direct option set that proves the contract, normally: --tool=memcheck, --leak-check=full, --show-leak-kinds=all, --errors-for-leak-kinds=definite,indirect, --track-fds=yes, and a nonzero --error-exitcode. Enable origin tracking only for diagnosis because of its additional cost.
7. Treat invalid reads or writes, dangerous uninitialized use, invalid or double frees, definite or indirect leaks, bad descriptor use, and non-inherited leaked descriptors as failures. Report possibly lost and still-reachable allocations without failing the initial baseline, but classify their owner and exact stack.
8. Begin with no suppression. Add a suppression only for a reproducible non-Orbit runtime or upstream report after inspecting the exact stack and source. Keep each suppression narrow, named, justified, tied to the exact component version, and removable; never import an upstream suppression file wholesale or suppress Orbit-owned frames.
9. Run locally or as an explicit pre-dogfood check. Do not add it to every push, the existing default cost-bounded CI job, a schedule, or the full test suite. A later automation decision requires measured duration, stability, cost, and separate approval.
10. If Memcheck finds an Orbit-owned defect, preserve the trace, leave this Bead open, and stop for the appropriate contract and implementation scope rather than hiding it or widening this verification issue.

Portability disposition: Linux-only verification tool with no product portability consequence. macOS remains covered by its own platform proof strategy; this Bead makes no Valgrind-on-macOS claim.

No CHANGELOG entry is expected. Update the README LOC scorecard only if tracked handwritten test, script, or suppression text changes. Full generated logs remain untracked evidence artifacts; the Bead records the exact command, result summary, hashes where useful, and location.
acceptance_criteria:
1. orb-j0m.3 is closed at an accepted proof-bearing revision before work begins. The Execution baseline routes no new product contract and records the exact ORB-C1 through ORB-C9 revisions and the tracked surfaces this hardening slice may change.
2. A pre-edit Reference gate records exact Valgrind, libghostty-vt, libghostty-vt-sys, Ghostty, and Orbit identities; verifies the relied-on Memcheck and descriptor-option semantics; and preserves the user-selected direct Valgrind executable with no Cargo wrapper or dependency.
3. One deterministic bounded scenario starts the real Orbit server and child, attaches, produces representative VT output, resizes, scrolls, selects and copies, detaches, reattaches, exits the child, reaps processes, removes the owned socket, and exits Orbit cleanly.
4. The actual yazelix-orbit process and exact pinned libghostty code run under Memcheck with useful debug symbols. The evidence distinguishes the monitored server from Cargo, the harness, the shell child, and unrelated helper processes.
5. The exact Valgrind command and version are recorded. It performs full leak analysis, displays all leak kinds, returns nonzero for Memcheck errors and definite or indirect leaks, and enables file-descriptor tracking.
6. Invalid reads or writes, dangerous uninitialized use, invalid or double frees, definite or indirect leaks, bad descriptor use, and non-inherited leaked descriptors are zero. Any finding remains unsuppressed and blocks closure until assigned to an exact owner.
7. Possibly lost and still-reachable allocations are reported without failing the initial run. Each nonzero record is classified by exact stack and component; the result does not silently relabel it clean or convert it into a product memory claim.
8. The first run uses no suppression. Any later suppression is narrow, named, source-inspected, version-scoped, justified in the Bead, and absent from Orbit-owned frames. No broad or wholesale Ghostty, Rust, libc, shell, or Valgrind suppression set is accepted.
9. The check runs manually against the exact accepted revision before orb-j0m.4. It does not run on every push, on a schedule, over the complete Cargo suite, or in a new CI matrix, and it adds no cargo-valgrind, testing framework, product mode, or product binary.
10. If a small reusable command, script, test-harness seam, or suppression file is necessary, it is the minimum direct surface, has one exact self-check, changes no product behavior or protocol, and updates documentation and LOC accounting mechanically. A product fix or CI/Nix expansion stops for separate scope.
11. Canonical locked Rust and governance checks required by any tracked changes pass, along with git diff --check. No runtime contract is promoted solely from planning or a Memcheck report.
12. Closure records the proof revision, platform, tool and dependency identities, exact command, scenario, elapsed time, error and leak summaries, descriptor result, suppression inventory, generated-log location, changed LOC, limitations, and one outcome: clean enough for orb-j0m.4, or held open with one named owner defect.
notes:
Completed repository-hardening proof at Orbit revision 6452a2f4f4233a7a89a17e479eda36b010516dcf. This changes no product contract or proof status; it hardens the accepted ORB-C1, ORB-C2, and ORB-C4 through ORB-C9 implementations without changing docs/CONTRACTS.md.

Ownership and minimum shape: tests/lifecycle.rs remains the protocol-faithful lifecycle owner. One ORBIT_MEMCHECK opt-in wraps only the existing CARGO_BIN_EXE_yazelix-orbit subprocess with the direct Valgrind executable. The existing selection lifecycle gained six history rows and one checked scroll-back/scroll-forward cycle, while retaining resize, Unicode VT output, selection/copy, detach, reattach, alternate screen, child exit, server reap, and socket cleanup. No product Rust, protocol, manifest, dependency, framework, binary, product mode, CI, Nix surface, or CHANGELOG entry changed.

Accepted runner and dependencies: Pop!_OS 24.04, Linux 7.0.11-76070011-generic x86_64; rustc/cargo 1.96.0; Zig 0.15.2; libghostty-vt 0.2.1 checksum 6219ed1c364b3ef5815fb0fd2acc0662f792adc706dabf59b7ca89280ee6d066; libghostty-vt-sys 0.2.1 checksum 865fed12a8b2bba3507b3bccd0bef439e06ef1100e652fe6b71d132c41ee8db0; Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083; Ubuntu Valgrind 1:3.22.0-0ubuntu3 with matching libc6-dbg 2.39-0ubuntu8.8 extracted locally. Cargo and direct dependency footprints are unchanged.

Exact proof command: env LIBGHOSTTY_VT_SYS_OPTIMIZE=Debug CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=2 VALGRIND_LIB=/tmp/orbit-valgrind-glibc.mDIsXI/valgrind-root/usr/libexec/valgrind VALGRIND_OPTS=--extra-debuginfo-path=/tmp/orbit-valgrind-glibc.mDIsXI/root ORBIT_MEMCHECK=/tmp/orbit-valgrind-glibc.mDIsXI/valgrind-root/usr/bin/valgrind cargo test --locked --test lifecycle selection_copy_is_authoritative_bounded_and_client_scoped -- --exact --nocapture

Result: pass; focused scenario 2.00 seconds and full command 3.07 seconds wall time. target/orbit-memcheck.2117204.log SHA-256 13ee93762282d910225252aed538c5e2970393fa2be0ff33e1f9395b34f58cbf records 0 errors, 0 definite/indirect/possible lost bytes, 544 still-reachable bytes in Rust stack-overflow thread_info runtime state, and only three stdio descriptors plus Valgrind own per-process log descriptor. target/orbit-memcheck.2117208.log SHA-256 9a8fa45f683769e026a7e1412983eb5b6967151213e68aed97f759d9079b37c6 is the pre-exec PTY child log; child tracing stops at shell exec. Suppression inventory: none.

Rejected: Valgrind 3.27.1 from Nix because its fd tracker falsely treated the libc::openpty slave descriptor as never created; cargo-valgrind, whole-suite tracing, shell tracing, imported or local suppressions, new tooling surfaces, CI automation, and product changes. The rejected trace remains target/orbit-memcheck.2111955.log.

LOC: tests/lifecycle.rs +33/-11, net +22 owned Rust; README scorecard is product 7,183, governance 765, total 7,948.

Verification at 6452a2f: cargo fmt --all --check; cargo check --locked --workspace; cargo test --locked --workspace; cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .; target/starcompass/bin/starcompass check-consumer with the four repository inputs; cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings; git diff --check. One initial workspace test run transiently hit ConnectionRefused in the unchanged stale-socket test; its exact rerun and the complete workspace rerun passed.

Limitations: one manual Linux lifecycle is not a blanket memory-safety or macOS claim; the shell child is intentionally outside Memcheck after exec; the Rust runtime reachable allocation is reported, not relabeled as freed; generated logs remain ignored target artifacts. Outcome: clean enough for orb-j0m.4.

title: Advertise the Eon terminal identity
description:
User-approved correction for the orb-j0m.4 dogfood gap. Orbit currently sets TERM=xterm-ghostty for every PTY child, but the accepted development and dogfood environment does not install that terminfo entry, so clear and other terminfo consumers fail.

Create ORB-C10: every Orbit PTY child advertises TERM=eon, and the accepted launch environment supplies the repository-owned eon terminfo entry. Keep the initial capability profile conservative by inheriting the installed xterm-256color record while Orbit continues to use libghostty and COLORTERM=truecolor. This is a PTY child-environment behavior change, not an ORBS or ORBF protocol change; Venus remains unchanged.

Scope: one two-line terminfo source, the existing TERM assignment, the minimum current launch documentation, focused real-PTY proof, the contract index, and required LOC scorecard update. No dependency, build framework, runtime installer, compatibility alias, configuration surface, terminal-profile abstraction, packaging system, remote support, or Venus change.
design:
Contract and implementation shape:

- ORB-C10 consumer: every program spawned inside an Orbit-owned PTY. Trigger: PTY child spawn. Result: TERM=eon resolves through the accepted launch environment to a compiled Eon terminfo entry whose initial capabilities are the conservative xterm-256color baseline; COLORTERM remains truecolor. Important failure: launch is not accepted if eon cannot be resolved or clear fails.
- Source owner: terminfo/eon.terminfo. Orbit owns the advertised identity in src/platform.rs. Eon distribution will later install the same source into its runtime closure; this Bead adds no packaging surface.
- Required before code: pinned Ghostty a887df42 terminfo identity and build behavior; installed ncurses tic/terminfo primary documentation and xterm-256color entry. Comparison only: the absent xterm-ghostty entry and a no-custom-name fallback. Rejected scope: copying Ghostty's generated capability table, runtime materialization, custom feature deltas, remote propagation, configuration, and aliases.
- First falsifying check: compile the source with tic into an isolated directory, resolve eon with infocmp, launch a real Orbit PTY with that TERMINFO directory, and prove TERM=eon plus a successful clear sequence.
- Platform disposition: isolated Linux terminfo dependency; macOS packaging is unproved, but the source format and tic workflow are portable. No ORBS/ORBF or Venus compatibility change.
acceptance_criteria:
1. terminfo/eon.terminfo contains one Eon entry inheriting xterm-256color, with no duplicated capability table.
2. Orbit sets TERM=eon for every PTY child and keeps COLORTERM=truecolor.
3. tic -x compiles the source into an isolated terminfo directory; infocmp resolves eon and shows the inherited baseline.
4. A real Orbit-owned PTY launched with that directory reports TERM=eon, clear exits successfully, and the shell remains usable.
5. README documents the current one-command terminfo installation before running Orbit. The later Eon package remains explicitly responsible for installing the same entry rather than gaining a speculative packaging implementation here.
6. docs/CONTRACTS.md records ORB-C10 and exact proof status without changing ORB-C1 through ORB-C9 or the Orbit/Venus protocol boundary.
7. No dependency, build script, installer, runtime extraction, alias set, configuration, protocol, Venus, remote, or compatibility layer is added.
8. README LOC scorecard reflects tracked handwritten project files, and canonical Rust, governance, clippy, terminfo, real-PTY, and git-diff checks pass.
9. Closure records the exact proof-bearing commit only after the accepted revision exists; until then evidence remains candidate.

title: Transfer rich terminal graphics through a bounded resource plane
description:
## Approved contract direction

Decision date: 2026-08-12.

Consumer: Venus rendering an attached Orbit session.

Trigger: Orbit's authoritative libghostty state contains a static Kitty image and one or more resolved placements.

Result: Orbit advertises one bounded static-graphics capability, sends decoded RGB or RGBA resources through a separate chunked resource plane, and refers to them from complete presentation state by opaque epoch-scoped image identity and libghostty generation. Venus validates, uploads, caches, places, and evicts those resources without parsing Kitty escapes or reconstructing terminal state. A missing resource causes a bounded request or resync, never silent omission.

Important failures: malformed metadata, dimensions or decoded size above the negotiated bounds, allocation or queue pressure, stale generations, missing chunks or resources, GPU eviction, resize, screen transition, detach, reconnect, and process exit remain explicit and bounded. Graphics work cannot block PTY processing or create unbounded retained state.

## Contract routing

- The user approves changing ORB-C6 and adding one permanent static-graphics resource contract. The first Orbit implementation child must assign and index the new ORB-C* ID before code.
- Preserve ORB-C1 through ORB-C5 and ORB-C7 through ORB-C11. Orbit remains the sole Kitty parser and terminal/image-state owner. Venus owns native validation, GPU resources, cache, and drawing.
- Replace ORBF v1 and the then-current ORBS revision atomically with their next canonical revisions. Serialize this work after any earlier protocol-changing issue. Update Orbit first, then Venus, then the pinned Eon/Eonova runtime. Add no adapter, dual decoder, compatibility window, or feature probe for an older revision.
- Planning this epic changes no contract index or runtime behavior.

## Evidence and selected references

Required before code:

- Current Orbit presentation, protocol, owner loop, lifecycle tests, contracts, and reference map at the execution baseline.
- `libghostty-vt` 0.2.1, crates.io checksum `6219ed1c364b3ef5815fb0fd2acc0662f792adc706dabf59b7ca89280ee6d066`, plus its exact published C API and source. Its storage and placement iterators, decoded pixels, resolved geometry, and generation stamps are the candidate owner mechanism.
- The official Kitty graphics specification at an exact revision chosen at the reference gate.
- Yazi commit `3518b9daac2c8b981fca232fa030996be1eda404`, whose KGP driver sends direct chunked raw RGB or RGBA and current `a=T,C=1,U=1` placeholders.
- Nova Zellij commit `bbccdea6eda81f314151160f9b3f8882a26478ec`, MIT. Nova pins this fork, and its tested current-Yazi translation makes Eonova a valid end-to-end acceptance path. The user confirms that this fork already renders Kitty graphics correctly.
- Venus and Eon at their implementation baselines.

Comparison only:

- Ghostty commit `a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083`, MIT. Adopt its separation of authoritative image storage, decoded pixel access, resolved placements, and generation-based invalidation. Reject its same-process renderer, application architecture, and unneeded protocol breadth.

## Selected first slice

- Static images only.
- One real producer path: Yazi image previews through the pinned Nova Zellij fork in Eonova.
- Direct, chunked raw RGB and RGBA ingress already handled by libghostty. The presentation plane carries decoded pixels, not Kitty commands or encoded source media.
- Ordinary placements and the exact current Eonova/Yazi path after libghostty resolves terminal semantics. Venus receives image identity, generation, source rectangle, resolved viewport geometry, pixel format and dimensions, and z-order needed for static composition. Venus does not interpret placeholder glyphs.
- Replace, delete, clear, scroll, resize, primary/alternate-screen transition, detach, reconnect, missing-resource recovery, and GPU eviction.
- Opaque session-epoch image identity plus libghostty generation. Do not add content hashing unless later measurement proves repeated decoded uploads dominate and generation identity cannot solve it.
- Exact numeric limits for images, dimensions, decoded bytes, chunks, outstanding transfers, queue occupancy, and Venus cache memory before allocation.

## Outside this slice

- Animation frames, animation control, composition, timing, video, and audio.
- General Unicode-placeholder semantics beyond the pinned Nova Zellij/Yazi path, including separate virtual placements, placement IDs encoded in underline color, alternative image-ID encodings, sparse or overlapping grids, source-cell selection, and relative placement chains.
- PNG or another image decoder added by Orbit, file or temporary-file transport, shared memory, persistence across Orbit restart, remote storage, Sixel, iTerm2 graphics, or a general multimedia framework.
- Kitty parsing or hidden terminal-state inference in Venus, a second terminal engine, a libghostty fork, or embedding image payloads in every complete frame.
design:
## Implementation shape

This issue remains a planning epic and is never the implementation unit.

1. Create a bounded API-proof child. Pin the exact `libghostty-vt` source and prove that the public API exposes decoded RGB/RGBA resources, stable image identity and generation, resolved visible placements, deletion, screen transitions, scroll, resize, and safe lifetimes. Measure extraction and retained-memory cost. Stop before a fork or binding extension if it does not.
2. Create one Orbit owner child. Index the approved contract, choose the next available ORBF and ORBS revisions after earlier protocol work, define exact quotas, and implement the smallest resource messages plus placement references. Use session-epoch identity and libghostty generation; do not hash pixels.
3. Create one Venus consumer child. Validate resource metadata and chunks before upload, keep one bounded GPU cache, draw resolved static placements, and request or resync missing resources. Add no Kitty parser or terminal model.
4. Create one Eonova acceptance child. Pin the proved Orbit and Venus revisions and dogfood Yazi previews through Nova Zellij `bbccdea6eda81f314151160f9b3f8882a26478ec` across scroll, resize, delete, alternate screen, detach, and reattach.

First check: against the exact pinned libghostty build, feed Yazi's current direct raw RGB/RGBA stream and inspect the authoritative active-screen storage and placement iterators after transmit, placeholder placement, scroll, resize, delete, alternate-screen transition, and reattach-equivalent snapshot. Record pointer lifetime, generation behavior, decoded byte ownership, lookup cost, and peak retained bytes. If any required lifecycle state is unavailable or ambiguous, stop before wire design.

No new dependency is selected. A decoder, hash, compression, cache, allocator, or binding dependency requires its own Crate gate and user approval.

Portability: neutral protocol. GPU upload and platform limits remain isolated in Venus. Any borrowed-pointer or native-resource assumption that cannot support a future macOS client is a stop condition, not a compatibility layer.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The approved ORB-C6 change and new static-graphics contract are indexed before production code, and the Bead records the exact Orbit-to-Venus-to-Eon/Eonova update order.
2. Negotiation is exact: a supported client receives the bounded static resource contract; an unsupported client gets an explicit capability result. No authoritative visible placement is silently dropped.
3. Canonical codec checks cover the next ORBF and ORBS revisions, resource announcement and chunks, placement references, requests or resync, deletion, and all declared bounds. Old, malformed, truncated, trailing, oversized, stale, duplicate, and out-of-order values fail deterministically.
4. Complete frames contain placement references without repeating image payloads. One decoded resource is transferred at most once per client epoch and generation unless eviction or loss causes an explicit bounded recovery.
5. Orbit exposes only libghostty-owned decoded RGB/RGBA and resolved placement state. Venus neither parses Kitty commands nor interprets Unicode placeholder cells.
6. Exact limits cover resource count, dimensions, decoded bytes, chunk size and count, outstanding transfer bytes, output pressure, and Venus GPU cache memory before allocation. Slow or broken consumers cannot block PTY processing or retain unbounded work.
7. Focused lifecycle proof covers replacement, deletion, clear, scroll, resize, clipping, z-order, primary and alternate screens, missing resource, GPU eviction, detach, reconnect, and exit without stale placements or false success.
8. Linux Eonova dogfood renders Yazi image previews through Nova Zellij `bbccdea6eda81f314151160f9b3f8882a26478ec` with correct geometry and lifecycle across scroll, resize, delete, alternate screen, detach, and reattach.
9. The proof records extraction cost, transfer bytes, peak Orbit decoded-image storage, peak Venus GPU cache, queue pressure, exact source revisions, unsupported Kitty features, portability disposition, LOC, and canonical locked checks.
notes:
Priority P3 and deferred. The static slice is useful, but it should not preempt the active protocol frontier. User approval selects the contract direction and removes the former scope-decision stop; it does not activate implementation or approve a dependency, fork, binding extension, or alternate terminal engine.

`orb-bi4.7` is closed, so it is historical planning context rather than a live blocker. Graphics remains independent of scrolling and ordered effects. Serialize protocol revisions instead of coupling their behavior.

Rejected: full Kitty parity, animation, general Unicode placeholders, content-addressed resources, pixel bytes in every frame, a client-side Kitty parser, unbounded caches, restart persistence, a graphics framework, and treating the epic as an implementation unit.

Effort L. Risk HIGH because resource bounds, lifetime, wire compatibility, and GPU consumption cross repositories. Confidence MED until the exact published libghostty API passes the first check.

Do not create implementation children until the user activates this deferred epic. At activation, use only the four children named in the implementation shape; split further only if the API proof finds an independently owned blocker.

Accept the pinned Nova Zellij/Yazi path as the real Eonova target; the fork already works with Kitty graphics. This approves planning scope only and does not activate implementation or approve a dependency, binding extension, or fork.

title: Separate coalescible terminal state from ordered effects
description:
Contract routing:
- Requires a new user-approved effects contract before implementation; this planning Bead reserves no permanent ORB-C* ID.
- Preserves ORB-C1, ORB-C2, and ORB-C4 through ORB-C11 while changing the client-facing ORBS boundary. ORB-C11 already owns one bounded clipboard-write effect; additional effect classes remain separately approved scope.
- Requires a separately owned Venus consumer contract and exact compatible-or-breaking update order. Planning this Bead changes no contract index or runtime behavior.

## Why

ORBF complete frames are intentionally replaceable latest state. Bells, clipboard writes, notifications, and similar terminal effects are ordered events and cannot inherit frame coalescing without silent loss or duplication. Conversely title, working directory, and latest progress are state and should not become an append-only event log. Terminal-generated PTY responses are a third class and must remain on the authoritative Orbit-to-PTY path rather than entering either client plane.

## Evidence

- docs/RATIONALE.md records distinct Snapshot, History, Effects, Resources, and Actions planes and assigns ordered effects to Orbit.
- README.md identifies a separate ordered effect stream as the preferred later direction requiring a user-approved decision.
- src/main.rs:140-154 installs the sole authoritative on_pty_write callback in the current owner loop.
- libghostty-vt and libghostty-vt-sys 0.2.1 pin Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083. Its C bridge always installs the device-attributes trampoline; without a custom callback it returns default attributes, and the terminal encodes DA1, DA2, and DA3 replies through writePty. Orbit therefore already captures those default replies through on_pty_write.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs` has the accepted ORB-C11 clipboard-write message but no bell or notification message.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md` proves one bounded ordered clipboard-write effect; it does not prove a general effect plane or any additional effect class.

## Scope

In scope:
- Classify terminal outputs into coalescible state, ordered effects, terminal-generated PTY responses, and unsupported capabilities.
- Add bounded effect identity, ordering, delivery, overflow, detach, reattach, and version-mismatch semantics.
- Capture supported libghostty effects without blocking its synchronous callbacks.
- Keep default DA1, DA2, and DA3 responses on the existing authoritative PTY-response path. A custom advertised terminal identity or capability set is a separate product-policy choice, not an effect.
- Preserve ORB-C11 clipboard ownership. Keep native policy and delivery for every additional approved effect in the highest owner with platform/user context; Orbit owns terminal interpretation and bounded transport.
- Coordinate an Orbit protocol/runtime proof followed by a separate Venus consumer proof.

Out of scope:
- Snapshot-plus-patch optimization, full history, graphics resources, remote delivery, durable event logging, notification history, custom terminal identity policy, or terminal effects replayed after an unobserved disconnect.
design:
## Implementation Notes

1. Add the user-approved effects contract before code and classify the ORBS change as compatible or breaking for every known Venus consumer.
2. Complete the Execution baseline and Reference gate. Required before code: the exact then-current libghostty effects and callback source, Ghostty BEL and OSC 52 behavior, notification and progress protocols where exposed, and one exact structured-terminal comparison such as WezTerm. Reject their unrelated multiplexer and UI scope.
3. Classify every output before adding a callback or message. Preserve accepted ORB-C11 clipboard writes as ordered effects. Treat current title, CWD, and progress as latest state; treat bell, notification, and attention requests as ordered effects only when the authoritative engine exposes them; retain engine-generated query replies on `on_pty_write`.
4. DA1, DA2, and DA3 are terminal-generated PTY responses under ORB-C2. The pinned 0.2.1 bridge supplies default attributes when no custom on_device_attributes callback is registered and emits the encoded response through on_pty_write. Do not add a second DA encoder, client message, or effect. Register on_device_attributes only after a separately approved terminal-identity or advertised-capability policy requires non-default values.
5. Keep effect callback work bounded and nonblocking. Copy only validated bounded payloads into the Orbit owner loop.
6. Define event IDs, revision association, acknowledgements only where they serve a contract, and explicit behavior for queue pressure, disconnect, reconnect, and gaps. Never silently coalesce an ordered effect.
7. Land the canonical protocol and Orbit proof first. A separate Venus Bead then consumes the exact proof and owns native delivery and permission UX.

Dependency decision: prefer the existing standard library and libghostty APIs. Any direct crate or feature expansion requires the Crate gate before manifest edits.

Portability disposition: neutral effect values and ordering; clipboard, notification, and desktop delivery remain isolated Venus/platform concerns.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if libghostty lacks the required public callback or state API; record the exact missing surface.
- Stop if a synchronous callback would require blocking on Venus or user input.
- Stop for user choice before custom terminal identity or capability advertisement, any breaking protocol revision, or a compatibility window.
- Stop if bounded pressure cannot preserve the selected per-kind semantics without explicit failure.

Comparison-only evidence: Canario RioEngine.swift at Rio 3e41b8b19a1cad9cd9bdfc8f7900cf61ce5a9098 immediately writes librio clipboard callbacks to NSPasteboard. Treat that as the concrete policy-coupling failure the Orbit/Venus split must avoid, not as accepted clipboard behavior or a required architecture.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The effects contract is approved and indexed before implementation, and all affected ORB-C contracts plus known Venus consumers have an explicit compatibility and update plan.
2. One contract table classifies each supported output as coalescible state, ordered effect, terminal-generated PTY response, or unsupported capability with exactly one owner.
3. DA1, DA2, and DA3 remain single authoritative terminal-generated PTY responses through the existing on_pty_write path. title: Transport bounded terminal clipboard writes to the attached client
description:
Contract: introduce ORB-C11. When the authoritative terminal parses an OSC 52 or normalized equivalent write, Orbit emits one bounded ordered clipboard-write message to the currently attached ORBS client. Orbit owns interpretation and transport; Venus owns native clipboard policy and delivery. Detached writes are not retained or replayed. Unsupported representations, embedded NUL, clears, and payloads above the existing 1 MiB copy bound are rejected before admission.

Compatibility: this is an owner-first breaking ORBS v2 to v3 replacement. Existing accepted messages retain their layouts, but the exact revision advances because current Venus cannot consume the new server message. Orbit proves v3 first; a separate Venus bead and run must consume its exact proof before Eonova acceptance. No adapter, dual decoder, or compatibility window.

Scope: existing libghostty callback, one plain-text clipboard write effect, existing bounded non-coalescing output queue, exact protocol and real-PTY proof. No native clipboard access, readback, permissions UI, BEL, notification, replay log, generic effects framework, or new dependency.
design: Use libghostty-vt 0.2.1 on_clipboard_write and the existing Orbit owner loop. Admit only exactly one non-empty text/plain representation whose UTF-8 bytes are at most MAX_COPY_BYTES and contain no NUL; preserve its normalized standard, selection, or primary destination. Copy admitted writes into a count-and-byte-bounded FIFO only while a negotiated ORBS client is attached. After each PTY read, queue every effect as a non-coalescible ServerMessage before the resulting coalescible frame. An effect handoff or client-output overflow disconnects the client, making the delivery gap explicit; detached writes are denied and never retained. Advance the canonical session protocol atomically to v3; preserve all earlier message layouts.
acceptance_criteria:
1. ORB-C11 is indexed before code and records the breaking v3 producer-first update order.
2. The canonical codec round-trips a destination plus UTF-8 text and rejects oversize or invalid payloads.
3. A real PTY OSC 52 write reaches the attached client exactly once and in queue order without becoming a frame.
4. Detached, unsupported, clear, binary or NUL, oversize, and full-output-queue writes are not retained or replayed; the synchronous callback stays bounded and nonblocking.
5. Existing ORB-C1 through ORB-C10 behavior remains covered and locked Rust checks pass.
6. The proof commit, references, remaining Venus consumer gap, LOC scorecard, and changelog disposition are recorded; br is flushed.
notes:
Accepted result: ORBS v3 Orbit producer proof 3ee7c80005f3d2bbe81e539799327803716f6174 implements ORB-C11. Orbit owns terminal interpretation and ordered bounded transport; Venus remains the sole owner of native clipboard policy and delivery. The breaking v2-to-v3 update has no adapter, dual decoder, feature probe, or compatibility window. ORB-C1 through ORB-C10 remain covered.

Implementation: reuse libghostty-vt 0.2.1 on_clipboard_write, the synchronous owner loop, and OutputQueue. PendingClipboardWrites owns the negotiated-client gate, 64-entry FIFO, cumulative 1 MiB bound, and terminal overflow state. It admits one non-empty UTF-8 text/plain representation with a valid standard, selection, or primary destination. Effects queue before the same PTY-turn frame. Detached writes return Denied and are never retained; handoff or output pressure disconnects instead of silently dropping an admitted effect.

Safety and dependencies: Cargo metadata and the dependency graph are unchanged. The pinned safe binding is unsound for a null zero-length clear and binary-safe non-UTF-8 data, so Orbit uses one compile-checked raw-pointer seam for exact libghostty-vt 0.2.1, validates pointers, bounds, MIME bytes, destination, UTF-8, and NUL before allocation, and never calls the unsafe contents iterator. Remove the seam when the binding exposes a safe byte-oriented view.

Proof: focused canonical-codec, callback admission, output-pressure, and real-PTY tests cover valid normalized destinations, invalid and oversize values, terminal batch pressure, detached denial, ordered delivery before the same-turn frame, and exactly once through the final Exited sentinel. Verification at the proof revision passed cargo fmt --all -- --check; cargo check --locked --workspace; cargo test --locked --workspace with 54 tests; cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .; Starcompass check-consumer; cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings; git diff --check.

LOC and disposition: product Rust and tests 7,564; governance Rust 765; total owned Rust 8,329; terminfo 2; total implementation source 8,331. Protocol package 3,228 lines: 2,195 production and 1,033 tests. The accepted changelog entry and contract index name the proof revision. Protocol and owner-loop behavior remain platform-neutral.

Remaining separately owned work: Venus at 2d36c72dc87ca5416e22d6afdc35c6ab4e2fb832 consumes ORBS v2, so native delivery and Eonova runtime acceptance remain open. Pinned libghostty allocates OSC 52 parser storage before the callback; bounding that pre-existing allocation requires a separate upstream allocator or binding decision. Clears, empty, invalid UTF-8 or NUL text, multiple or non-text representations, reads, BEL, notifications, replay, remote transport, and native permission UX remain unsupported.

title: Provide native mobile access to Eon sessions
description:
## Outcome

Provide a real native mobile Eon client that reconnects to durable Orbit sessions and materializes Orbit-authored structured presentation with mobile-native interaction. This is the preferred mobile experience for touch, software and hardware keyboards, IME, clipboard, accessibility, graphics, lifecycle, and narrow-screen workspace navigation.

The client is not a terminal emulator wrapped around raw PTY bytes and is not an SSH-terminal skin. Orbit remains the sole terminal authority.

## Contract routing

- This deferred epic is a planning container. It changes no ORB-C, EON-C, or VEN-C contract, reserves no contract ID, chooses no repository or mobile framework, and authorizes no code, dependency, listener, remote endpoint, distribution channel, or platform promise.
- At activation, approve and index separate contracts for secure remote attachment, Eon workspace/mobile product behavior, and the first native client platform before implementation children are created.
- Preserve Orbit as the sole PTY, parser, terminal state, viewport, selection, copied text, effects, graphics-resource interpretation, and terminal-query authority.
- Preserve Eon as workspace/session identity, topology, attention, authorization policy, orchestration, composition, and distribution owner.
- The mobile shell owns platform lifecycle, rendering, touch and keyboard collection, IME, clipboard delivery, accessibility, notifications only if separately approved, and ephemeral view state.
- Eon Desktop remains desktop-only and Venus is not automatically the mobile shell or repository. Activation must choose the mobile code-owning repository and platform owner explicitly without copying Venus or creating a shared UI framework by default.
- Preserve the one-active-client rule unless multiplayer is separately chosen. Native mobile does not imply simultaneous Venus attachment.

## Boundary

The native client consumes the canonical versioned Orbit presentation/session boundary over a separately approved secure remote carrier. It validates and reduces Orbit-authored state, renders it natively, and sends semantic interaction. It does not parse raw PTY output, answer terminal queries, infer hidden terminal state, scrape terminal text for Eon policy, or maintain a second handwritten protocol schema.

Remote transport/authentication and mobile presentation are distinct responsibilities even when delivered by one product slice. Activation must compare using standard SSH as a carrier or tunnel, a direct authenticated transport, and no remote implementation; it must not assume the permanent SSH-terminal client is the transport foundation.

A mobile client needs two logical owner planes: Eon-authored workspace snapshots/actions and Orbit-authored presentation/semantic interaction. A secure carrier may multiplex them, but it cannot merge their schemas, authorization, lifecycle, or state owners. EONW v1 contains host-local opaque Orbit endpoint bytes; those bytes must never cross the network, become global session identity, or be interpreted by the client. The remote Eon boundary must expose authorized stable product identities or capabilities that the host resolves to local Orbit endpoints.

## Initial product limits

- Choose one initial mobile platform and proof device at activation. Preserve a credible second-platform boundary without promising iOS and Android simultaneously.
- Start with one active mobile client attached to one selected live session inside the accepted Eon workspace model.
- No multiplayer, offline terminal execution, Orbit/machine restart persistence, remote workspace provisioning, repository synchronization, general file browser, plugin framework, or web compatibility layer.
- Graphics may remain an explicit unsupported capability until the separate bounded graphics plane is accepted; silent loss is forbidden.
- Native mobile and SSH terminal access remain independent permanent surfaces. Native mobile may become preferred without deleting SSH fallback.
- The first proof may use a development-signed device install. App Store, Play Store, TestFlight, public signing, review, billing, telemetry, push infrastructure, and general distribution remain separately approved scope.

## Success Criteria

- One explicitly selected mobile platform proves a secure native real-device client over canonical Orbit state and Eon workspace identities.
- Touch, keyboard/IME, clipboard, accessibility, lifecycle, and reconnect behavior are native and bounded without a second terminal authority or protocol schema.
- SSH fallback remains independently useful; the native client becomes preferred mobile UX without coupling or retiring it.
design:
## Activation shape

Do not implement this epic directly. When activated, split it by repository and failure domain:

1. Product/contract decision: choose the first platform, target device, smallest mobile workflow, exact Eon workspace/session actions, one-client behavior, security boundary, and proof matrix.
2. Secure remote-attachment owner: reuse any accepted shared remote-attachment contract already serving Eon Web or another client. If none exists, create one owner-first transport child rather than a mobile-specific protocol. Compare standard SSH stdio/tunneling, a direct mutually authenticated transport, and no remote transport. Define authentication, authorization, endpoint discovery, host-side mapping from remote capabilities to local Eon/Orbit endpoints, negotiation, replay resistance, confidentiality, integrity, bounds, cancellation, reconnect, revocation, version mismatch, and observability before exposing any listener.
3. Remote Eon control boundary: prove a client can inspect and act on authorized workspace identities without receiving EONW v1's host-local endpoint bytes, duplicating Eon topology, or broadening actions silently. Keep Eon control and Orbit presentation as distinct logical planes even if one carrier multiplexes them.
4. Canonical client core: consume the exact orbit-protocol package and reducer without a second schema or terminal engine. Keep protocol semantics in Rust where practical; expose only a coarse validated state/action boundary to the platform shell.
5. Platform shell and renderer: implement only the chosen first platform's lifecycle, native rendering, touch/keyboard/IME, clipboard, accessibility, geometry, and ephemeral navigation.
6. Eon integration: consume Eon-owned workspace/session identities and actions without reconstructing topology or attention from terminal content.
7. Cross-repository acceptance: prove secure loss/reconnect, process survival, coherent reattach, semantic input, resize/rotation, background/foreground transitions, resource pressure, accessibility, and real-device use.
8. Remote efficiency decision: measure complete-frame bytes, latency, CPU, memory, and convergence on fixed representative Wi-Fi and constrained-link profiles with a correctness oracle. Keep existing bounded complete-frame coalescing if it passes. Only a measured failure may activate a separate Orbit patch, feedback, or resync contract; do not prebuild one for mobile.

## Platform-language gate

Do not select Swift/SwiftUI, Kotlin/Compose, Flutter, React Native, a shared Wasm renderer, or another framework from preference alone. Compare native platform tools, reuse of the canonical Rust core, and credible cross-platform candidates against lifecycle correctness, input/IME, accessibility, text and grapheme rendering, GPU/graphics, binary/dependency cost, debugging, distribution, and second-platform replacement cost.

A first Apple-native shell may choose Swift/SwiftUI around a narrow Rust boundary when the selected iOS proof shows a measurable platform advantage. Android receives its own explicit platform choice; shared product/protocol semantics do not require shared UI code.

## Security and lifecycle

Remote access is a trust boundary. Before code, define who authenticates the device and user, which Eon workspace/session actions are authorized, how credentials are stored and revoked, what is exposed on the network, and how negotiation fails closed. Bound all messages, resources, queues, retries, backoff, background work, and client storage.

Client disappearance never transfers terminal authority or kills the PTY while Orbit remains running. Mobile backgrounding, suspension, process death, rotation, network changes, stale credentials, Busy, incompatible versions, remote Orbit exit, and host loss must produce deterministic recovery or terminal failure without orphan work.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The epic remains deferred and unclaimable for implementation until the user chooses an initial mobile platform/proof device and approves indexed remote-attachment, remote Eon control, and mobile product contracts.
2. Activation chooses one mobile code-owning repository. Eon Desktop remains desktop-only unless the user separately changes that boundary; shared Rust protocol code does not imply shared native UI code.
3. The mobile client consumes canonical Orbit protocol/reducer state and Eon-owned workspace/action identities at exact accepted revisions; it contains no raw-PTY parser, second terminal emulator, handwritten mirror schema, or terminal-query responder.
4. Orbit remains the sole authority for terminal state, viewport, selection/copy text, effects, graphics interpretation, input encoding, and PTY lifecycle. Eon remains the sole workspace/topology/action/authorization-policy owner.
5. Eon control and Orbit presentation remain distinct logical planes. EONW v1 host-local endpoint bytes never cross the network or become remote identity; the host alone resolves an authenticated stable identity or capability to a local Orbit endpoint.
6. A pre-implementation security decision defines carrier, authentication, authorization, credential storage and revocation, endpoint exposure/discovery, capability-to-endpoint resolution, confidentiality, integrity, replay/version failure, bounds, and cleanup. No listener is exposed before this proof.
7. The transport owner is shared with any accepted Eon Web or other remote client boundary when their contract matches; the mobile epic does not create an independent parallel remote protocol. The permanent SSH-terminal client is neither required nor treated as the native renderer.
8. One chosen initial mobile platform proves a native real-device workflow for inspecting the authorized Eon workspace, selecting one live session, coherent attach, semantic typing and keys, IME, touch/pointer interaction, paste and clipboard delivery, resize/rotation, background/foreground, network loss/reconnect, Busy, session exit, and client-process death.
9. Native text, style, grapheme, cursor, title, hyperlink, accessibility, and capability behavior is explicitly tested or declared unsupported. Graphics remain explicit until the accepted bounded resource plane is consumed.
10. Queues, frame/resource memory, retries, backoff, reconnect, background work, and local client storage are bounded; slow or malicious remote input cannot block Orbit's authoritative PTY processing.
11. Fixed representative Wi-Fi and constrained-link measurements record complete-frame bytes, latency, CPU, memory, and convergence against a correctness oracle. A patch/feedback/resync protocol is activated only if the accepted complete-frame path fails a predeclared bound.
12. The one-active-client rule remains enforced. Simultaneous Venus/mobile use, observation, takeover, and multiplayer are rejected unless separately approved.
13. The first platform choice does not force platform UI APIs into the Rust protocol/core or promise the second platform. Its replacement and second-platform boundary are recorded.
14. Owner transport, remote Eon control, canonical client core, platform shell, Eon integration, and final acceptance are separate children with exact compatibility/update order and proof revisions.
15. The first proof may use a development-signed install and makes no public-store promise. Acceptance records exact device/OS, carrier and endpoint, security evidence, lifecycle observations, accessibility/input/graphics limits, performance/resource bounds, dependencies, owned LOC, installation method, distribution limits, and remaining platform gaps.
notes:
User decision: native mobile is a later preferred experience alongside, not instead of, permanent SSH terminal access.

Priority P3, effort XL, implementation risk high because remote trust, native rendering/input/accessibility, application lifecycle, and cross-repository compatibility are distinct proof surfaces.

No dependency on the SSH-terminal epic is intended. The mobile transport decision may reuse standard SSH as a carrier if evidence supports it, but it must not inherit a lossy ANSI projection or require the SSH-facing Eon client.

Planning references: orb-bi4.7 ownership and language direction; ORB-C1 through ORB-C11; canonical orbit-protocol reducer; Eon workspace/action contracts; orb-j2i for future graphics resources; Herdr only as evidence for the value of phone reconnect, not as the native architecture.

Cross-repository prerequisites: activation must pin exact accepted Eon workspace/action and Venus comparison revisions. Track Eon `eon-pxn` and `eon-pxn.3`, plus Venus `ven-c87` as the current thin-client ownership proof. Venus is evidence, not the presumed mobile implementation owner.

Prime-beads disposition: the shared remote-attachment contract is a prerequisite plane, not a third product experience. Reuse one accepted owner across native mobile and future Eon Web when their security contract matches; keep their presentation/lifecycle clients separate.

title: Decide the minimal permanent Orbit Formatter proof
description:
## Contract routing

This is a planning-only verification decision. It changes no ORB product contract, test suite, dependency, or documentation. Any chosen test reduction requires a separately authorized implementation Bead.

Consumer: Orbit maintainers relying on executable evidence for the sole-authority terminal architecture.

Trigger: reassess the permanent value of the Formatter reconstruction experiment after Orbit's authoritative-state design, ORBF/ORBS contracts, and Venus consumer have been accepted.

Result: choose and record the smallest executable Formatter regression set that still protects a live contract or a material dependency assumption; preserve non-executable rejected-design evidence in its canonical documentation owner.

Important failures: do not remove the sole-authority regression cited by ORB-C2 without equivalent proof; do not keep experiments solely because they already exist; do not turn historical negative evidence into an unsupported memory claim.

## Why

`tests/formatter_attachment.rs` is 281 lines containing eight tests and shared helpers. Most tests repeatedly demonstrate that reconstructing a second terminal from libghostty Formatter output loses state. That architecture has already been rejected and recorded in `docs/RATIONALE.md` and `docs/CRATES.md`. Only `only_authoritative_terminal_emits_pty_responses` is cited directly by the current ORB-C2 contract row, but the other tests may still guard dependency behavior worth retaining.

Impact: LOW. Investigation effort: S. Decision risk: LOW-MED. Confidence in shrink opportunity: MED-HIGH.

## Evidence

- `tests/formatter_attachment.rs:90-280`: eight executable experiments cover inactive screens, modes/palette/input, cursor and hyperlinks, charsets, pending wrap, split parser state, title/Kitty graphics, PTY responses, and scrollback/reflow.
- `tests/formatter_attachment.rs:242-257`: the compact sole-authority regression proves that only the authoritative terminal emits a PTY response.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:29`: ORB-C2 cites `only_authoritative_terminal_emits_pty_responses` as canonical evidence.
- `docs/CRATES.md:12`: the accepted libghostty decision already records Formatter reconstruction as a rejected alternative.
- `docs/RATIONALE.md:140-145`: durable architecture prose records why Formatter output cannot reproduce hidden terminal state.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- Record the exact Orbit and `libghostty-vt` revisions under review.
- Read every test and its helpers, every repository reference to the file/test names, the ORB-C2/ORB-C4/ORB-C6 proof rows, and the accepted terminal-authority decision.
- Inspect the exact libghostty Formatter API and relevant upstream tests/source for the pinned version. Determine whether each local negative test protects a current upstream assumption, a current Orbit contract, or only the historical selection experiment.
- Check whether stronger real-PTY, lifecycle, presentation, or protocol tests already fail for the same meaningful regression.

## Scope

In scope:
- `tests/formatter_attachment.rs` and every direct documentation/contract reference to its evidence.
- Current libghostty Formatter behavior relied on by the accepted architectural rejection.
- Existing Orbit tests that may subsume each negative experiment.

Out of scope:
- Editing tests or documentation.
- Reopening Orbit's one-authoritative-terminal architecture or replacing libghostty.
- Weakening ORB-C2, PTY-response ownership, terminal-state fidelity, rich-presentation, or attachment proof.
- Adding a new test framework, snapshot corpus, dependency, or generalized conformance suite.
- Auditing unrelated lifecycle or presentation tests.

## Decision method

1. Map each test to a live product contract, dependency assumption, rejected alternative, or historical-only observation.
2. Identify the cheapest existing test that would fail if each live invariant regressed.
3. Compare retain-all, retain a minimal subset, retain only the sole-authority regression, and archive all negative evidence as documentation.
4. For a shrink decision, name every retained and removed test/helper and the exact documentation/proof updates required.
5. Estimate net LOC, test runtime, maintenance burden, and proof loss for each shape.
6. Select the first sufficient shape and record the condition that would justify restoring a broader Formatter experiment suite.
7. Create no implementation Bead without separate user authorization.

## Acceptance

- All eight tests are classified individually; no test is removed by category-level assumption.
- Every live ORB contract and terminal-authority invariant retains executable coverage.
- Historical negative findings remain durably attributable to the inspected libghostty revision even if their executable reproductions are retired.
- The decision explicitly chooses retain, shrink, or delete and lists exact retained evidence.
- If shrinking to one test is selected, the record proves why the other seven no longer buy unique regression detection.
- The decision records exact LOC/test-time consequences, rejected shapes, reversal conditions, and whether later implementation work is warranted.

## Verification

- `cargo test --locked --test formatter_attachment` should establish the current eight-test baseline.
- `rg -n 'formatter_attachment|only_authoritative_terminal_emits_pty_responses|Formatter' README.md docs src tests .github Cargo.toml` should enumerate current consumers of the evidence.
- Run the exact overlapping test commands identified during the mapping and record which live invariant each proves.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0; implementation and documentation files must remain unchanged.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue for this Bead.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only authorized planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the pinned libghostty version or Formatter behavior changes during investigation.
- Stop if removing any candidate test would leave a live contract or dependency assumption without a cheap executable check.
- Stop if deciding requires changing the accepted terminal-authority architecture.
- Stop if evaluating a candidate requires editing repository files.

## Maintenance notes

The target is not an arbitrary LOC quota. Preserve the smallest test set that catches a plausible regression in current behavior; keep historical architecture evidence as prose tied to its exact inspected revision.
